FITZPATRICK (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 132) to amend the Railway Act, 19U3.
Will the hon. gentleman explain ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill is for the purpose of meeting a difficulty that was suggested during the course of the discussion on the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill with respect to the apportionment of freight rates as between two companies operating under a joint traffic arrangement. It was suggested that the Railway Commission had not full control over such an arrangement. I was of opinion at the time that they had that control ; but after looking at the Act, I think that the control would be only with respect to companies operating in Canada, and would not be . applicable to companies operating partly in Canada and partly in the United States. Nor do I think the provisions of the Act go far enough to be applicable to a transportation company operating on the great lakes and under the

control of a foreign corporation. That Is tlie tlrst amendment. The second is as to the nationality of the directors of subsidized railways in Canada.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I desire to ask the Minister of Labour if the parties to the strike in Sydney, Nova Scotia, have request ed the intervention of the department, or if the minister himself has volunteered any assistance in that matter ?

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. gentleman, I have to say that neither of the parties to the dispute at the Dominion Iron and Steel Company's works at Sydney has invited the intervention of the government or the Department of Labour. The Sydney Board of Trade did so, and overtures were made by the department to both parties ; but up to the present moment neither of the parties has been willing to avail itself of the services of the department. I have the correspondence here, and, if the House will allow me, I will read it. The following is a telegram from the Sydney Board of Trade :
Sydney, C.B., June 1, 1904, The Hon. Minister of Labour,
Ottawa.
The Sydney Board of Trade, at a meeting held to-day unanimously resolved to ask your intervention in the existing trouble between the Dominion Iron and Steel Company and its employees, which has resolved itself into a general strike that threatens to very seriously affect this community. Briefly stated, the employees' contention is that they are not receiving a living wage, or their just proportion of the bounties paid by your government to the company. The company, on the other hand, contends that it is paying average wages, and offers to arbitrate upon this point. The Board of Trade has therefore passed the following resolution :-That, in view of the large bounties paid by the government to the iron and steel industries in Canada, the government be requested to intervene along the following lines, namely, to require the company to show the condition of its affairs to such persons as the government may see fit to appoint, with a view either, (a) to convince the employees that the company is not yet in a position to accede to their demands for higher wages, or, - (b) to bring such pressure to bear upon the company as will lead to an immediate settlement of the existing difficulties.
(Sgd.) S. P. CHALLONER, Secy., Board of Trade.
In response to this the following communication was sent to the vice-president of the company, the president, I understand, being at present outside of the country :
Toronto, 2nd June, 1904,
Dear Sir,-The government much regrets the existing differences between the Dominion Iron Mr. FITZPATRICK.
and Steel Company and their employees and which have resulted in a strike and a shutting down of the works and earnestly hope that at the earliest moment harmony may be restored and the men be again at work.
The Sydney Board of Trade has telegraphed asking intervention of the Department of Labour, and I beg to offer the department's services' towards a settlement of the differences. Yours faithfully,

Minister of Labour
F. Nicholls, Esq.,
Vice-president, Dom. I. & S. C.,
Toronto.
To this the following answer was received:
14-16 King St., East,
- Toronto, Canada June 3rd 1904.
Sir William Muloclc, K.C.M.G..
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa.
Dear sir,-I beg to acknowledge, receipt of your letter of the 2nd inst., and may say I share your regret at the existence of differences between the Dominion Iron and Steel Company and their employees. At the time of reorganization of the company's affairs last December, the position of the company was fully explained to the representatives of the men and also to members of the town council and Board of Trade of Sydney, and there has been no change for the better in the iron and steel market since that date. The trend of prices has been steadily downward, and ironmasters have in some cases shut down their works and in others reduced their staff of employees and also their wages. We have made a determined effort under discouraging circumstances to keep the various mills in operation and afford continued employment to our workmen. A short time since they made a demand for increased pay, which, under the circumstances, it is impossible to concede, but as with this demand was coupled the statement that they were receiving less than the standard rate of wages in similar industries, our directors in their reply offered to submit this claim to arbitration, and I inclose a copy of the resolution adopted unanimously by the directors at a special meeting called to consider the situation.
As the men have voluntarily quit work, the company has decided to suspend operations until the iron and steel trade is in a more satisfactory condition, but with a sincere desire to alleviate any possible suffering, arrangements have been made to, so far as possible, give work to any of our late employees w'ho may desire It.
Yours faithfully
(Sgd.) FREDERIC NICHOLLS,
Vice-president Dominion Iron and Steel Co.
He inclosed in that letter the following-copy of the resolution referred to :
Copy of a resolution unanimously passed by the directors of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company :
At a meeting of the board held on Monday, May 30th, 1904, it was resolved that the director of w-orks be authorized to ask the officers

of the P. W. Association and a committee of the employees of the company to meet the president and himself on Thursday, the 16th day of June next, and to say to them that the directors of this company are of opinion that they are now paying the current rate of wages beyond what it at present is and that in event of the P, W. Association and the committee of the employees disputing the correctness of this statement as to the rate of wages, that the company will consent to a decision thereon by a board of arbitrators to be chosen, one by the company, one by the employees, and an umpire to be chosen by these two, and failing the choice, that he be a judge of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia named by the lieutenant governor.
I also sent tlie following telegram to Mi Moffatt :
(Telegram.)
Toronto, 3rd June, 1904.
John Moffatt,
Grand Secretary, P.W.A.,
Sydney, N.S.
Sydney Board of Trade has telegraphed government suggesting its intervention with view to removal of present troubles between Dominion Iron and Steel Company and its employees. Government greatly regrets existence of these differences, and hope that without jlelay satisfactory solution may be found, and if desired will be pleased to lend its friendly services towards removing grounds of friction and reestablishing friendly relations between both sides. Kindly telegraph me whether intervention by government agreeable to employees, directing answer after to-day to me at Ottawa.

Minister of Labour.
To this telegram the following reply was received :
Dominion, N.S., June 4.
Hon. Wm. Muloclc,
Ottawa.
We prefer to be left to settle this dispute ourselves in our own way. Thanks for kind offer.

On the 4tli of .Tune I sent the following telegram to Mr. Challoner :
(Copy)	June 4, 1904.
S. P. Challoner,
Secretary Board of Trade,
Sydney, N.S.
On request of Sydney Board of Trade I offered to both parties friendly intervention of Department of Labour in present dispute between Iron and Steel Company and their employees, but greatly regret that replies received indicate unwillingness to accept government intervention. Am mailing you to-day copies of correspondence.
(Signed.) WILLIAM MULOCK.
On the same day I forwarded the copies of the correspondence, accompanied by the following letter :
(Copy)

June 4, 1904.
re Request of Sydney Board of Trade for intervention of Department of Labour, in dispute between Dominion Iron and Steel Company and its employees.
Dear Sir :
As promised in my telegram to you this morning, I am inclosing you herewith copies
of correspondence between the government and the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, and the representative of its employees, in regard to the communication received from the Sydney Board of Trade, asking the intervention of the Department of Labour, with a view of bringing about a settlement of existing difficulties.
Upon receipt of your telegram I immediately offered the services of the department to both parties, but greatly regret that the replies received indicate an unwillingness to accept government intervention.
It is possible that the parties to the dispute may not desire the immediate intervention of any third party, hut that later on they may change their attitude in this particular. In which event I shall be only too pleased to lend the friendly offices of the department, should such intervention be acceptable.
Yours faithfully,
WILLIAM MULOCK, Minister of Labour.
S. P. Challoner, Esq.
Secretary Board of Trade,
Sydney, N.S.

Before the Orders of the Day are proceeded with I would call the attention of the House to the fact that the Public Accounts Committee has not met for some time. I do not know whether this is due to the unavoidable absence from the city of the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade), who is chairman of the committee. But we wish the committee to be convened as soon as possible.

I have been absent from the city for a couple of weeks, and I suppose it is owing to that fact that the the committee, has not been convened. But, in addition, there did not seem to be any business before the committee. I will have the committee summoned at once, probably Wednesday.

House again in committee on Bill (No 110) respecting the Ottawa Electric Company-Mr. Champagne.
On the preamble and amendment (Mr. Sproule) that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

This Bill I regard as a very obnoxious Bill and one that ought not to be passed. Through this Bill, the Ottawa Electric Company is trying to escape ah obligation that it owes to the city of Ottawa, namely, not be a party to consolidation with other companies in the same business. It now seeks to evade that res-ponsibilty and to secure the power of merging other companies and so to create a monopoly in this city. We have long heard it said in this House that competition was a great protection of the public. Competition, we were told many times, was the life of trade. Following that principle the people of Ottawa tried to secure competition and

prevent consolidation. Now, apparently, tilings liave changed, and combination is being effected, and, I am sorry to say is being aided in this House. The doctrine of the Liberal party at one time was, as I said, that competition would cure all the evils that humanity complained of. But, now, as I said the great doctrine of the Liberal party is combination in the interest of these monopolies. Another thing that I regret to notice is that the government is trying to escape responsibility for the conduct of the committees of this House. Not long ago, I drew attention to this fact ; and now I wish to read a quotation bearing on this subject. The late Sir John Bourinot has dealt with the question of the responsibility of the government for the action of the committees of the House, and his opinion must carry weight. I have here 1 The Life of Lord Elgin,' by Sir John Bouriont. At page 247, I find the following:
The Canadian minister

Meaning, of course, the Prime Minister.
-having control of the finances and taxes and of all matters of administration, is directly responsible to parliament and sooner or later to the people for the manner In which public functions have been discharged. All important measures are initiated by the cabinet, and on every question of public interest the ministers are bound to have a definite policy if they wish to retain the confidence of the legislature, *Even in the case of private legislation they are also the guardians of the public interest and are responsible to the parliament and the people for any neglect in particular.
He goes on to say
Responsible government makes the premier and his ministers responsible for the constitution of the committees and for the opinions and decisions that may emanate from them. A government that would constantly endeavour to shift its responsibilities on committees, even of its own selection, would soon disappear from the treasury benches. Responsibility in legislation is accordingly ensured financial measures prevented from being made the footballs of ambitious and irresponsible politicians and the impartiality and indignity of the Speakership guaranteed by the presence in parliament of a cabinet having the direction and supervision of business.
Now, we have that doctrine of responsible government in this country-at least, I hope we have. I hope we believe in it. Under that doctrine the government of the day are responsible for tire conduct of these committees, and particularly are responsible for all legislation that goes through this House, and so cannot evade responsibility for legislation passing through this House that is in the interest of monopoly and against the interest of the people. Now, this Bill is clearly in the interest of monopoly, as against the interest of the people, and it is being put through the House by the government of the day. Every vote in favour of this monopoly when it was Mr. MACLEAN.
considered in committee on Private Bills, was a Liberal vote. The three whips of the government were engaged in that committee in trying to put this Bill in favour of monopoly through the House. X simply take my stand on the doctrine of responsible government, and I point to the fact that this legislation is legislation in the interest of monopoly and not in the interest of the people, and I say that the government of the day are responsible-either they must protect the rights of the people against monopoly or they must stand convicted of dereliction of duty.
There is another point with regard to this Bill. Something must be added, if it is to be allowed to go through the House, and later on, I intend to move an amendment in that direction. We are hearing today a great deal about the principle of public ownership. It is the new evangel of this century.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
I am glad to say I have been one of those who have been preaching this evangel.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only thing In which the hon. gentleman has been consistent.

It Is an excellent gospel. It is an excellent doctrine, and is making great beadway in this country. But if the evangel of public ownership is to make any headway, it must apply the principle of public ownership on every occasion, it must apply it in municipal affairs, in provincial affairs and in federal affairs. There is only one way to do it, and it is a practical way and that is to' adopt the principle of public ownership by putting a purchase clause in every private Bill of this kind that goes through either the provincial legislature or this federal House ; and no council in any municipality to-day will be discharging its duty to itself, no council in any municipality will be discharging its duty to its constituency unless it insists on this purchase clause being In every one of these private Bills. Now, If a man is in favour of public ownership, I don't care whether he be a Liberal or Conservative, if he does not support that proposition, he is not sound in regard to public ownership. I intend to propose in this Bill that the Ottawa Electric Company should be compelled to adopt a clause that I have drafted, and which I will submit later on. Let me give a specific instance where this clause was adopted. In 1891, the Kingston Gas and Electric Company was incorporated at Toronto. The clause read :
But at any time from and after the expiration of twenty years from the passing of this Act-
I would change that a little and make it 12 months.

-the corporation of the city of Kingston shall have the right, on giving twelve months notice to the Kingston Light, Heat and Power Company of such their intention, to expropriate the works and property of said company under and in accordance with the provisions of the general Act.
And so on. Now, if'tliis Ottawa Electric Company is in the public interest, as they say they are, it will be willing to have that clause put in this Bill, and I propose to put it in, just as the Kingston Light, Heat and Power Company liad to submit to its being put iu their Bill. Further, I am advised that this company said some time ago that it the city of Ottawa desired to expropriate it under the Conmee Act, they would be willing to do so. I am not able to say whether they can expropriate it under the Conmee Act or not. It might be interfering with Dominion legislation unless this Act is incorporated under Dominion law. But to avoid all that, I propose to have this purchase clause put in this Act of the Ottawa Electric Company, and, as 1 said before, that would be a real test of public ownership in this country. The real test of public ownership in municipal politics will be the insertion of a purchase clause in every agreement made between one of these private companies holding a public franchise and the municipality; the test will be that the legislature of Ontario, by a general Act, and this legislature, in so far as it has jurisdiction in these cases, shall put this purchase clause in every one of these Acts. Now, down in the province of Quebec, they have had some experience with these private companies. In a newspaper called ' La Fresse, ' published in Montreal, and edited by Mr. Dansereau, there was a significant article of which I will read one or two paragraphs. It was an editorial appearing on June first:
The session of the Quebec legislature for 1904 has been particularly remarkable and marked ; if custom declared that we must christen each session, this last one is certainly entitled to be called the session of the electrical trust.
Every measure throwing a shade on the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company or on the surburban street car lines, has been pitilessly rejected ; every measure favourable to this formidable trust has heen adopted. Never before has a cabal as cynical, as brutal, been organized at Quebec. Ministers, magistrates and a cloud of lawyers have been in the service of the electrical trust and have exercised a deplorable pressure on our lawmakers.
The same thing has happened here iu Ottawa. A cloud of lawyers, a cloud of lobbyists In the interests of this corporation, and a cloud of whips in the service of the Liberal party, have been working in the interest of this corporation, and the rights of the people are being taken away from them in the interest
Where were you that day ?
I was away, and I am here to-day. Where was the hon. gentleman?
I was not away.

How did the kon. gentleman vote ? The hon. gentleman voted in the interest of the monopoly, he backs up his party to-day in the interest of the monopoly. I am here to fight monopolies to-day, ai*d I will fight them, and the hon. gentleman will be in the cellar when the fight comes on. Now, Mr. Chairman, these companies are all powerful in the municipal councils, they are all powerful in legislatures, especially in legislatures that are controlled by Liberals, and they are all powerful in this House ; and we are asked to-day to strengthen this monopoly iu the city of Ottawa. Ottawa seems to be the peculiar home of a lot of grafters, the men who happen to hold stock in what I call the sawdust bank of this country. They are all more or less in the sawdust business, and they all think that the way to strengthen their monopolies
The sawdust men are on the other side.

I am not sure about that. But their policy is to be shining lights in Ottawa society and give a certain number of dinners every session, and in that way they think they can get any legislation they desire in this country in the interests of monopolies. Now, I say there is somebody else in this country who have interests to be protected besides those who are said to be capitalists, and who are in favour of monopolies-there are the people, and are the people's rights not worthy to be protected ? Or are the people's rights to be raided, as they have been raided in this legislature, as they are being raided by this Bill ? I think they are entitled to protection, and the way to protect them is to compel this company who are asking for this legislation, to accept the purchase clause. Here is the clause that I referred to, and which I propose to put in this Bill :
4. The powers hereby conferred upon the company are granted upon the condition that the corporation of the city of Ottawa shall have the right to acquire by expropriation the works and property of the company, and such right is hereby conferred upon such corporation subject to the payment of compensation by the said corporation to the company to be determined, in the event of failure to agree, by arbitration in the manner provided for by the clauses' of ' The Consolidated Municipal Act, 1903,' of the province of Ontario relating to arbitrations, and the amount of such compensation shall be estimated by the arbitrators so to be appointed in the manner provided for by clause (a3) of subsection 4 of section 566 of the said last mentioned Act, which said subsection is commonly referred to as the ' Conmee Act,.
Here is the provision I propose to insert in their Bill. We will give this company the power they ask for to increase their capital, we will give them the power to buy out this

other company, but in giving them these powers we will impose upon them this condition, that the city of Ottawa shall have the right to purchase this franchise on a valuation.
Why didn't they make that a part of the contract ?
Because of the cloud of lawyers and lobbyists who surrounded their municipal council when these amendments were going through.
Will the hon. gentleman say that the* people want government ownership Why did'nt the people oppose the Bill ?
They have tried to get public ownership but whenever they do try to get it a cloud of lawyers, some government whips and some ministers line up their followers to defeat public ownership.
Where are the people ?
The people demand public ownership. .
Then why don't they get it ?

They have been blocked time after time, but they are going to get it. All these municipalities are going to have public ownership, and that is what wc are going to have in the city of Toronto. The people in England have it to-day and they have it because they have obtained the legislation which they desired in that direction from parliament which was favourable to the proposition, but in some way public ownership in this country is. considered to be a crime by the political parties, is considered to be socialistic, as I have said before in this House. Now, all that is changing and I say : Give the people the power to expropriate this company. In the city of Ottawa the people have had a hard fight against the monopolistic companies.
Does not the Ontario law provide for that ?

I do not know if it does because the Ontario law may not reach a Dominion Act. I am making provision by which the people of Ottawa, under this federal Bill, will have secured to them the right to purchase the property of this company.
Have you given any notice of .this amendment ?
I have not given it in committee but this is substantially giving notice of it.	..
What do the council of the city of Ottawa say about this ?
They have uot declared upon it yet but they will declare upon it.
I am giving them an opportunity to protect themselves.
Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen have a great faculty of saying ' hear, hear ' and laughing when anybody proposes anything in the public interest, but you ought to see them - run to give $175,000,000 of the people's money to the- Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. They shine upon occasions of that kind, but whenever anything is proposed in the interest of the people they oppose it like my hon. friend from British Columbia who says he is a socialist. He i's everything. He is a workingman's candidate
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I have never said that I was a socialist.

Well, we will change that. He has assumed to speak in the labour interest of this country and I can tell him that the labour interest is in favour of public ownership. I would like him to go to the city of Toronto and state to the working men of that city that public ownership is a delusion and a snare.
I believe in municipal ownership, but I want the hon. gentleman to give some evidence that the people desire it. If the people of Ottawa desire it why do they not get it ?

I will tell you why. The people of Ottawa voted a while ago for public ownership of the telephone system. They voted for it twice and the city council declared for it two or three times and yet in some way some of the men who are working for this monopolistic corporation turned up in the interest of the Bell Telephone Company and the people were defeated. The public press of the city of Ottawa has been recreant towards the people iu regard to public ownership because in that respect they have abandoned the people and are aiding the corporations.
The people are greater than the press.

Yes, . the people are greater than the press, they are going to realize the situation and they are going to demonstrate that they are in favour of public ownership and in favour of a purchase clause. It takes the people some time to find out what the situation really is.
But the hon. gentleman says they believe in it.

The}7 do believe in it, and they are voting in favour of it. This House will eventually vote iu favour of it [DOT]and'the hon. gentleman ppposite will have an opportunity of showing whether lie is in favour of this legislation or not and he will have an opportunity of showing whether he

is in favour of this monopolistic corporation.
If the people of the city of Ottawa demonstrate to me that they are in favour of this legislation I will support it.

I am going to go one better and I am going to say that the people of Ottawa shall have the right by law to take over this concern if they wish to do so. Now, who is the chief consumer of electricity in the city of Ottawa ? I hold it is the people of Canada represented by the government of the day. The government is the chief revenue producer of this company in Ottawa and what are the relations between the government and this company today ? It has not even a contract with the company. It has given it the right to supply electrical energy and light and it renewed the first agreement it made with the company without competition and without any inquiry in regard to the price. It is paying to-day a price which it should never pay for electrical energy in Ottawa. Who gives this company the water privilege from which this power is generated ? The people of Canada. Who are entitled to fair treatment and reasonable prices for electrical light and power ? The people. Can the right lion, leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his party justify the absence of a contract with this company ensuring to the consumers a fair price? Can they justify themselves being a party to this legislation here which means a merger and which, if a merger takes place, empowers this Ottawa Electric Light Company to put up the rates ? They cannot justify it and I say as the chief consumers of electrical energy in this country and as those who have to pay the monthly bills of this corporation they should say : In our own interest we insist that there shall be no such merger. We will hold you strictly to your agreement. It has been stated in the committee that companies can find ways of getting around all these clauses designed to prevent consolidation. If that is so we ought to do what we can to strengthen the hands of the people by inserting this purchase clause. Some hon. gentlemen may have heard to-day perhaps, for the first time in regard to this purchase clause, but on every occasion upon which I can raise it I propose to raise it and to have it inserted in all this legislation dealing with these agreements. It ought to be inserted in all contracts of the same character made with this government that at any day upon giving due notice and paying a price to be settled by arbitration, the government can step in and take over the franchise,-or if a municipality is interested, the municipality may step in and take over the franchise and administer the service in the interest of the people. There is nothing so useful to the public as cheap electrical energy and we in
Canada have more electrical energy than ail the rest of the world put together. We have all the power that we require to drive all our railways, and all our machinery, to heat and to light all our houses, and we are doing nothing but giving it away to companies without any regulation as to the prices which they charge or as to treating the public fairly. Surely when we have this vast store of electrical energy and when we have no coal in many portions of the country we ought to take the greatest care to surround these grants with proper safeguards in the interest of the people. Nothing of that kind has been done in this country as yet. We have all been busy giving away concessions, giving away grants, giving away the people's money to these corporations without imposing sufficient regulations on them and without insisting upon some kind of a purchase clause agreement. 1 believe all that will be changed. I hope the government will see that it is responsible for this legislation, and especially that it will not try to shoulder the responsibility upon the committee, that it will assume the responsibility which belongs to it and that, as the chief consumer of electrical energy in the city of Ottawa, it will say to this company: We will not grant you this legislation allowing you to merge with another company. We will increase your capital if you want it increased but in the interest of the people of Ottawa we will impose upon' you the condition that they shall have the right to purchase if they desire it.

Mr. Chairman, we have been told by our hon. friends opposite that the city of Ottawa has entered no protest against the passage of this Bill. At the opening of this session of the House I presented a petition from the mayor on behalf of the citizens of Ottawa protesting against the present legislation.

Allow me to point out that the mayor of the city of Ottawa is not the council of the city of Ottawa. He is only one officer. What I asked my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) was if the council of the city of Ottawa had entered any protest against this legislation. So far, I as a member of this House have heard none.
The hob. gentleman must have heard the protest made on Friday about this very thing, and repeated again to-day.
Has any resolution from the city council of. Ottawa opposing this legislation, been placed before the House ?

In answer to the hon. gentleman's question. I may say that at the last meeting of the municipal council of the city of Ottawa a resolution was unanimously passed authorizing the mayor and the

city solicitor to look after the interests of tlie city in connection with this Bill. I have not a copy of the resolution at hand, but a copy was shown to me this morning by his worship Mayor Ellis.
What were the instructions contained in the resolution ?
I do not know the details, but the instruction was to look after the interests of the city in connection with this Bill.

I have a circular in my hand purporting to be issued by the mayor and city solicitor, representing that if this Bill should pass it would cause the city a loss of a quarter of a million dollars per year.
ilr. BIRKETT. So it will. Now that the bon. gentleman has brought that matter to my notice, I will explain how it will be a loss of a quarter of a million, or $300,000, a year to the citizens of Ottawa. In the first place, when the Ottawa Company got their franchise from the council of the city of Ottawa, the maximum price was one cent per ampere hour and twenty-five per cent discount, which for the purpose of calculation we may say that it was 75 cents per 100 amperes. When the Consumers Company and the Metropolitan Company got their franchise, that maximum rate was reduced to 52 cents per 100 amperes, and the price they are selling at to-day is 36 cents per 100 ampere hours. If the Ottawa Company should get the privileges they desire under this Bill, it is possible for them to increase the present rate of 36 cents per 100 amperes to 75 cents per 100 amperes. The revenue of the Ottawa Electric Company last year was $217,000 at 36 cents per 100 amperes, and the revenue of the Consumers Company was something in the neighbourhood of $80,000, or, both combined $300,000 in round numbers. Now, if 36 cents per 100 amperes will produce $300,000 and if they increase the price to 75 cents per 100 amperes, will it not produce $300,000 more, which will be an additional tax of $3uO,000 on the consumers of electric light and power in Ottawa ; a sum which is nearly one-half of our total taxes in the city ? I hope I have made that plain to hon. gentlemen. The petition which is placed in my hands and which I have the honour to present to the House is as follows :

When the House was summoned to the Senate I was about to read the following petition from the city of Ottawa :
To the honourable the House of Commons In parliament assembled :
The petition of the corporation of the city of Ottawa, humbly showeth :
1.	Bill No. HO ' An Act respecting the Ottawa Electric Company,' provides :-
(a.) That the capital stock of the company be increased from $1,000,000 to $1,500,000.
(b.) That the company may issue bonds to the amount of $1,125,000 instead of $500,000 as at present.
(c.) That the company may acquire shares in the capital stock, debentures, securities of other electric companies and that the proviso be struck out of the original Act which provides that such stock, debentures or securities shall only be issued ' as the consideration for goods, wares or merchandise sold to such other companies in the ordinary course of business.'
2.	In 1898 your petitioners granted a franchise to the Metropolitan Electric Company of Ottawa, Limited, authorizing that company to erect poles and wires for the purpose of supplying electric light and power. Maximum rates for electric light and power were fixed in that franchise.
3.	The following clause was inserted in that franchise :-
' 15. That the said company shall not at any time during the said period amalgamate or combine with any other company or companies now carrying on or which may hereafter at any time during the said period carry on in the said city of Ottawa, the business of supplying electricity for the purposes of power, light or heat, nor shall the said company enter into any contract, agreement or arrangement with any such company for such purpose or that shall have such effect, nor shall the said company enter into any contract, agreement or arrangement with any such company for the purpose, or that may have the effect of creating a monopoly of the business of supplying electricity for the purposes aforesaid in the city of Ottawa, without the permission of the council of the corporation of the city of Ottawa to be expressed by by-law.'
The purpose of this provision was to prevent the company obtaining the franchise from amalgamating or selling out to any other electric light company. The term of the franchise of the Metropolitan Company was for twenty-one years from 1898.
4.	The Metropolitan Company not having entered upon the business of supplying electric light, heat and power, your petitioners in 1901 gave a twenty-three year franchise to the Consumers' Electric Company, Limited. In that franchise the maximum rates- for commercial lighting and power were also fixed.
A similar proviso to that in the Metropolitan Company's franchise was inserted in the Consumers' franchise, providing that the latter company should not amalgamate or sell, out to any other electric light company.
5.	The object of your petitioners In granting, first, the Metropolitan franchise, and then the consumers' franchise was to secure competition in electric lighting with the Ottawa Electric Company. Your petitioners, at the "time these franchises were granted, relied on the provision in the Ottawa Electric Company's Act of incorporation, which provided that that company could only acquire the stock, debentures or securities of other electric companies ' as the consideration for goods, wares or merchandise sold to such other companies in the ordinary course of business.' It is now sought to have this protection to your petitioners struck out.
6.	When the Bill in question was before the Private Bills Committee an amendment was moved, that the power to purchase stock in other companies should not only apply to the stock of the Metropolitan or the Consumers' Company. This amendment was lost by 19 to 14. The refusal of the Ottawa Electric Company to accept this amendment indicates clearly that the real purpose of the Bill is to enable the Ottawa Company to buy out the Metropolitan and the Consumers' Company or one of them.
7.	Your petitioners are advised that the evident intention of the Bill is to enable the Metropolitan and the Consumers' Companies to get rid of the provisions against amalgamating or selling out to any other electric light company, which were inserted in these companies' franchises by your petitioners for the express purpose of securing competition, and consequently low rates for electric lighting.
8.	The rates charged at present by both the Ottawa Electric Company and the Consumers' Electric Company for electric light are about one-half less than they were before the Consumers' Company began to compete with the Ottawa Company. If the legislation now being asked for by the Ottawa Electric Company is granted, and it results in that company acquiring the Consumers' Company, the result will be that the citizens of Ottawa may have to pay from $250,000 to $300,000 every year more than at present for their electric light.
9 Your petitioners strongly submit that your honourable House should not enact legislation which will have the effect of taking away from the city the guarantee which it now has, that there will be competition in the supplying of electric light, heat and power, and consequently low rates.
10. The imposition of large rates for electric light, heat and power would not only compel the citizens of Ottawa to pay very much larger amounts each year for their light but they would have a deterrent effect upon any new industries coming to the city and would seriously retard the growth of the city.
11. In any event, your petitioners respectfully submit that the legislation now asked for



should not be granted on.the ground that parliament should not authorize a merger of any clas's^"of eompanies which would have the effect of creating a monopoly. .
12'. In the event of the Ottawa Company, the Consumers' Company and the Metropolitan Company being merged into one company, it would be very difficult, if not impossible, for any other company or your petitioners to enter upon the business of supplying electric light heat and power, because almost all the available water powers in the immediate vicinity of the city of Ottawa would'be in the hands of such a merger company or in the hands of persons or companies who could not supply power for the purposes of electric light, heat and power.
Your petitioners humbly pray that your honourable House will not enact the legislation asked for in clause 2 of the Bill of the Ottawa Electric Company, and that such clause should be struck out, or in any event that the Ottawa Electric Company should not be given authority to purchase the stock, debentures or securities of the Metropolitan Company or of the Consumers' Company.

I understand that somebody is moving that the preamble be declared not proven and I supposed that the main object of this Bill is to secure the authorization of an increase of the capital stock.
No, it is the coloured gentleman In the next clause.
If the preamble were rejected it would prevent an increase in the capital stock.

Does the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue hold that the city entered into a contract for its citizens to pay a certain amount to the Ottawa Electric Light Company for light and that it was obligatory upon them to take it at that rate?
Certainly.
Not at all.
There is a maximum price fixed by the contract.

The contract is simply to allow the electric light company to carry on their operations in the town, enabling them to construct works for that purpose and for the consideration they agree that they shall not charge the citizens more than a certain amount.
The contract is binding upon the city of Ottawa as well as upon this company.
Is the hon. gentleman arguing that the city is bound to take light at that price?
If the company is bound by its contract the city is bound by its contract.
Certainly it is, as far as the contract is concerned.

I am inclined to think that the city of Ottawa, by forming a new company and making a new contract, to a certain extent violated the old contract. But it does not matter, we are now dealing as between the city of Ottawa and the Ottawa Electric Light Company and suppose this Bill did pass there would be no violation of the contract except between the city and the company. My hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) spoke about municipal ownership. It has nothing to do with the Bill. I think he will realize, after the fine speech he has made upon municipal ownership, that it has no bearing at ail upon the question which is now before the committee. But, there is a point which has been raised by my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) to the effect that in this increase of capital for the purpose of subscribing stock in another company there is a violation of principle. I think in that respect my hon. friend is mistaken, because we have again and again passed legislation without any, objection giving to companies the right to subscribe to the capital stock of other companies.
The general law in Ontario gives this company the right to subscribe the capital stock of other companies of the same kind.
But this is not the case of parent subsidiary companies.
By section 79 of the Ontario Joint Stock Company's Act, if two-thirds of the shareholders consent they have a right to subscribe capital in any company.

The clause to which the hon. gentleman refers does not apply to the issue between the parties in this case, because if this company gets power to acquire the stock of the Consumers' Company the result will be great loss to the citizens of Ottawa. If the Minister of Inland Revenue argued on the supposition that the maximum price to be charged is the price now charged by the Consumers' Electric Company, then his quotation would be germane.

I am merely answering the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart), that the provision to enable them to subscribe stock in any other company was an extraordinary one. The hon. gentleman is mistaken as to that. Last session we gave three companies this power.
I did not say it was an extraordinary thing to allow one to take stock in another, but I pointed to the serious result in this case.

Last year we gave the Dominion Gas Improvement Company the same power as is now sought, and among the incorporators were Mr. MacDougall, Mr. [DOT] George Henderson, Mr. MacCormack and others, and we did not see the mayor and aldermen here to protest : The same power was given to three Ottawa companies last year by this parliament.

Is it not a fact that in all those cases the persons whose stock was to be acquired were the only parties affected, and had the sole right to say whether the stock should be acquired or not? In this case the Consumers' Electric Light Company was created by the city of Ottawa under agreement, and so long as the city of Ottawa, which is one of the parties to the agreement, objects to this *legislation, it is not fair for the Minister of Inland Revenue to cite such examples.

We gave the same power last year to the Canada Atlantic Railway Company, and there was no protest. For years this parliament has been giving similar powers to other corporations, and I do not see why the Ottawa Electric Company should be refused.

It is because, in this case, the people who will be adversely affected by it, entered a protest against the Consumers' Electric Light Company which they brought into existence being wiped out, and the maximum charge of the Ottawa Electric Company substituted for the maximum charge of the Consumers' Electric Light Company.

If there is any violation of contract, it is a violation on the part of the city of Ottawa, who, having entered into a contract with the Ottawa Electric Company, gave another contract to another company.

If it can be shown that the Ottawa Municipal Council was a party to giving an exclusive franchise to the Ottawa Electric Light Company. I shall vote for this Bill. I have only been able to glance at the contract, but I do not believe that there is any such provision in it. If the Ottawa Electric Company assume the rights of the Consumers' Light Company of the city of Ottawa, they should assume the obligation in the Consumers' Company's charter, and accept the maximum price which the Consumers' Company may charge.

If the Ottawa Company buys the stock of the Consumers' Company, they will be bound by the contract which exists between the Consumers' Company and the city of Ottawa. For my part I have no
other understanding about it. There is a contract existing between the city of Ottawa and the Ottawa Electric Company, and this Bill will not vary that contract. I do not see why we should not accord to the Ottawa Electric Company, the same treatment we have accorded to other companies time and time again.

I am glad to have the authority of a gentleman so eminent in the legal profession as the Minister of Inland Revenue for the statement that the amalgamation of these companies will oblige the amalgamated company to charge no higher rate than the maximum rate now charged by the Consumers' Electric Light Company.
It is nothing of the kind.

If the statement of the Minister of Inland Revenue is correct, then the interest of the light consumers of the city of Ottawa will be protected. If the Minister is perfectly clear on that point, why not insert such a provision in the Bill so as to make it beyond peradventure ?

I understand that the Ottawa Electric Company is willing to stand by the contract which it has with the city of Ottawa. If they buy over the Consumers' Electric Light Company, they will be bound by the contract between the Consumers' Company and the city.

It is not an amalgamation of two companies at all, it is an empowering Act to allow this company to purchase stock in the other. If this is passed, the Ottawa Company may purchase the whole of the stock of the Consumers' Company. It is true they would then be bound by all the obligations entered into by the Consumers' Company, but after the Ottawa Company acquires the stock of the Consumers' Company, the Consumers' Company would simply go out of existence. What is to prevent that ? What possible object would they have in working the two companies ? After the Ottawa Company acquires all the stock of the other company are they going to continue the two rates, one at 75 cents per 100 amperes, and the other at 36 cents ? The sole object is to Wipe out the company they purchase, and to carry on the business under the name of the old company.

Under the present legislation and without any violation of contract we, the largest consumers of this electrical energy, get electrical energy at a reduced price. Grant the legislation asked today and we will have to pay maximum prices. The Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Brodeur) made this proposition to the House and I never heard such a pettyfog-ging argument. It is as if I should agree with you, a grocer, to buy sugar at a maximum price of ten cents a pound. He says

that because I make that agreement I am prevented from buying sugar at four cents a pound from any one else. There is no violation at all on the part of the city of Ottawa. The city of Ottawa puts its statement most fairly.
The object of the city of Ottawa in granting, first, the Metropolitan franchise, and then the Consumers' franchise, was to secure competition in electric lighting with the Ottawa Electric Company. The city, at the time these franchises were granted, relied on the provision in the Ottawa Electric Company's Act of Incorporation, which provided that the city could only acquire the stock, debentures or securities of other electric companies * as the consideration for goods, wares or merchandise sold to such other companies in the ordinary course of- business.' It is now sought to have this protection to the city struck out.
The city of Ottawa and the people of Canada have a protection to-day in the purchase of this electrical energy, but grant the legislation desired and that protection is at once removed. The Ottawa Consumers' Company is empowered to put up the rates to a maximum of 75 cents. That is not in the public interest. Why should we give this company power to raid this House and the citizens of Ottawa. I ask the right hon. the Prime Minister, not as Prime Minister but as a citizen of Ottawa, does he think it is good legislation in the interests of the citizens ? Is it good legislation to remove this protection from the humblest citizen ? There has been no violation of the contract by the city of Ottawa ; they fulfilled their contract byi allowing the company to erect their poles and supply electricity, but now the company seeks to have removed a restriction that was placed in the contract in the interest of the city of Ottawa.

In the memorandum presented to us to-day, we find :
The rates on electric light provided for in the franchise given by the city of Ottawa to the Ottawa Electric Company and the Consumers' Electric Company are as follows :
Ottawa Electric Company. -75 of 1 cent per ampere hour net.
Consumers' Electric Company. -52 of 1 cent per ampere hour net.
What I desire to draw attention to is the next paragraph :
The present rates charged by both companies are *36 of 1 cent per ampere hour net.
If the suggestion made is accepted, the amalgamated companies could increase the rates from -36 of one cent to -52 of one cent per ampere hour, an increase of nearly 50 per cent. The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) pointed out this afternoon the result of the last year's operation under very difficult circumstances of the Ottawa Electric Company. We have not been able to get a statement of the last year's operations of the Consumers' Company, but I point out that if we pass this legislation ! Mr. Maclean.
the rate now charged by the Ottawa Company may be increased from -36 of one cent to -52 of one cent per ampere hour. The statement which the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) has presented shows that a very reasonable profit, on the investment has been made at the present rates. I would draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that the Consumers' Electric Company of Ottawa is composed of leading citizens of the city ; I am sure he would concur in that statement if he knew their names ; men who have a large interest in this community, men who did not go into that company simply as a toy, men who have made it a great success, and in view of that fact it is surely not unreasonable to say that when we give power to the Ottawa Company to absorb the Consumers, which is a fairly profitable concern, the obligations now imposed by the agreement between the city of Ottawa and either of the existing companies, should also be imposed upon the consolidated company.

I would like to have it clearly from the Minister of Inland Revenue in what way he makes out that the city of Ottawa are violating this agreement. The arrangement entered into between the city and the Ottawa Company was that the company would not charge more than 75 cents per 100 amperes. It is not a bargain it is an agreement made between the corporation of the city and the company, for the supplying of light to the citizens of Ottawa. They did not agree to take light at that price, but they agreed to give them certain privileges provided they supplied the light at that price and did not charge more. Then, when the Consumers' Company applied for a charter, that was a rival company that offered better conditions to the city. The city, not having given the Ottawa Company an exclusive franchise, said: What are your terms, what advantages are the citizens to dei'ive from incorporating a new Company V The company said : We will supply you with electricity at 52 cents per 100 amperes.
When the new company was formed or when the old company was formed ?

The new company was formed in 1901, and the old company got their amended charter in 1894. But there was no violation of an agreement, because the city had fulfilled their agreement by giving the company permission to erect poles and distribute electricity through the city.
My hon. friend Will admit that the Ottawa Company has the right to charge 75 cents ?

That it why we are fighting to-day. They can make money, under present conditions ; I showed a few moments ago that they made 7-22 per cent on

their capital selling light at 36 cents, and we do not wish them to be permitted to charge 75 cents. If this amalgamation is pe: mitted it may be that the Ottawa citizens .will have to pay 75 cents per 100 amper-es instead of 36 cents. .
Is the Consumers' Company opposing this legislation ?
We have not the Consumers' Company before us at all, but the city of Ottawa has a certain contract with the Consumers' Company and that we want to protect in the interest of the citizens.

On Friday night 1 stated my views on this matter, and I would not have troubled the committee again except for what has fallen from the lips of the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue. I am sorry to say that I cannot agree with his deductions. I am satisfied that the hon. minister did not read the whole Act of incorporation of this company, which we are being asked to amend, or he would not have drawn the deduction that the city of Ottawa is asking us to do anything unfair in refusing to pass section 2 of this Bill, which is for the purpose of amending section 7 ot the Act of incorporation. First, dealing with the minister's allegation that the city of Ottawa is trying to violate a contract made with this company by asking this House to refuse to pass this section, I wish to point out that the only effect of the amendment proposed to 'be made to section 7 is that a. restriction which was imposed by parliament on this company's right to buy up other companies, is to be removed. At the very most, the city of Ottawa says, leave us where we were in 1894, and leave the Ottawa Electric Company in the position in which they would be obliged to deal with us if they had not invoked new legislation. The city of Ottawa is asking for no special benefit for itself. It only asks parliament not to take away the restriction, whatever it is worth, which exists in the legislation of 1894 ; and when one opposes the amendment -which is intended to take away that restriction, surely it does not lie in tlie mouth of any one to say, you are asking that the city of Otta-wa be allowed to violate a contract. Section 8 of the statute of 1894 presupposes that this Ottawa Electric Company would want to buy up and amalgamate with it all the companies in existence at that time ; at all events, certain companies there named. It is quite clear that the Consumers' Company did not exist at that time ; it did not come into existence, I am told, until 1901 ; but the Chaudiere and the Standard Companies named in that statute did exist. What did the Act provide in regard to them ? What did this parliament solemnly declare should be done with respect to the companies that did then exist ? That the directors of those companies could sell out to the Ottawa Electric Company, and that it could buy their rights and franchises, but subject to this :
Provided that after any such purchase, lease or other acquirement, working arrangement or amalgamation as aforesaid is entered into, the company shall not, without the consent by bylaw or otherwise of t.h.j municipality of tho city of Ottawa or of the oily of Hull, respectively, as the case may be, Increase the ordinary prims or rates charged by any of.the said other companies for electric light in '.he city of Ottawa or in the city of Hull, respectively, at the time such purchase, lease or other acquirement, working arrangement or amalgamation is entered into.
That would not allow this company to buy up the companies that existed then except on condition that the rates in existence at the time of the amalgamation-not the maximum rates, as suggested by the Minister of Inland Revenue, but the rates brought about by competition or by any such force as the city of Ottawa within its rights could exercise-should not be exceeded, unless the city of Ottawa by by-law or otherwise agreed to something else. Talk about violations- where is the violation here, unless it is a violation by the Ottawa Electric Company, not simply of a contract with the city, but of an Act of parliament ? And why should this company have the right, under exactly the same circumstances, to amalgamate with the Consumers' Company without a similar provision being made applicable ? The Consumers' Company is not within that qualification of section 8, because it did not come into existence until four or five years afterwards. The only section that would apply to it would be subsection (d) of section 7 which we are asked to-day to remove. If we do not refuse to amend section 7 of the original Act, we should then, as an alternative, amend section 8 so as to include the Consumers' Company in the restrictive provision we made in 1894 with reference to other companies which were In the same position then that the Consumers' Company is in now. If this Bill passes without some such dealing with the Consumers' Company, what is the effect ? The effect is this, that the companies which are named in the Act of 1894 could not sell out to the Ottawa Company and charge higher rates than are there specified, without a by-law or agreement with the city of Ottawa, but this Consumers' Company, which came into existence in 1901, could do what we said the other companies should not be permitted to do. Therefore it seems to me that the Acts quoted by the Minister of Inland Revenue have no hearing on the case. I do not say that it is ultra vires of this parliament or wrong legislation in every case, to allow one company to buy up stock in another company. But I say that you must look at the circumstances of each case. This is all private legislation, based on an agreement between the city of Ottawa and the Ottawa Electric Company

in 1894, and if we allow this Bill to pass without some protection for the citizens of Ottawa, either by refusing to pass section 2, or by adding a clause to provide that the Consumers' Company shall be included in the provisions of section 8 of the original Act, we shall be doing away with the principle which this parliament declared should be carried out in 1894, when this Ottawa Electric Company was given its franchise permitting it to do business. To say that because the contract with the city provided for a maximum rate therefore that rate was agreed to by the city, is no argument at all. It is not common sense. That provision simply meant that the city wanted to get as cheap electricity as it could, and that it bound the company not to charge more than so much ; but it did not bind any one to pay that much if the electricity could be got at a cheaper price. The effect of this legislation, if passed without any amendment, must simply be that although the city of Ottawa has a right, by an Act of parliament which exists to-day, to prevent the Ottawa Electric Company from amalgamating with any other of the companies named in that Act, this Ottawa Electric Company could compel the city of Ottawa and its citizens to recognize rights in regard to other companies which have come into existence since 1894, and to deal with them on an entirely different basis from all other companies which were said to be seeking amalgamation with this company when the Act of 1894 was passed.

May I repeat, once more, the argument 1 have stated in this committee The government of the day are the guardians of the people's purse, the farmers of this country have put the government in charge of the purse of the nation. By legislation as it now exists, the people of this country are protected as to the rates they must pay for electric energy in the city of Ottawa. The Prime Minister, and the treasurer of this country, the Minister of Finance, so far as we can gather here to-day, arc deliberately in favour of removing this protection to the purse of the people. I ask the Prime Minister to bear that in mind. Also call his attention to this fact-that before any further steps are taken in connection with this Bill, we ought to have the Minister of Public Works here to tell us what we, as a nation, pay to this Electric Company in the city of Ottawa, that is now supplying this House and the various departments at Ottawa with electrical energy. The Minister of Public Works should be here to tell us whether we are getting as good a rate as the citizens of Ottawa are getting, and whether he would advise, as the one having the service in charge, that the protection that we have to-day should be removed. It is in the interest of the city, it is in the interest of the country, it is in the interest of the humblest consumer of electrical energy in the city of Ottawa, that this Mr. LANCASTER.
protection should be maintained. The removal of this protection is not in the interest of this company otherwise than as it strengthens its monopoly. We are supposed to be against monopoly in this country. We will grant the company all their rights ; but why should we give them more ? Parliament in its wisdom, some years ago, limited the company, limited them in the interest of the people of Ottawa, and, probably, of the people of Canada as represented by the government here. If that is the case, no matter what the privileges we may have given in other cases, these do not afford a reason why this protection now enjoyed by the people should be removed. That is the plain issue and I leave it here. We have a protection to-day against monopoly ; we have a protection against high prices for electrical energy,-and the proposal now is to remove that protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) point out the legislation that protects the people against monopoly, of which he speaks ?

The object of the city of Ottawa, in granting, first, the Metropolitan franchise and then the Consumers' franchise, was to secure competition in electric lighting with the Ottawa Electric Company.
The city, at the time these franchises were granted, relied on the provision in the Ottawa Electric Company's Act of incorporation, which provides that company could only acquire the stock, debentures or securities of other electric companies ' as the consideration for goods, wares or merchandise sold to such other companies in the ordinary course of business.' It is now sought to have this protection to the city struck out.
The protection is there, and the proposal is to strike it out. That is my contention, and it is the contention of the city.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I presume that my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) means that the protection is taken away by striking out the words in subsection D of section 7.
Let the minister read it himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I prefer, in an argument, to deal with one at a time. I presume that the hon. gentleman refers to the words in subsection D of section 7 ' as the consideration of goods, wares or merchandise sold to such other companies in the ordinary course of business. '
That is what the city says it relies upon.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was not in the committee when this Bill was under discussion, and am not informed as to the effect of this legislation, nor can I say that I have gathered a great deal of information from the discussion to-day. I take it that the objection is to the amendment of subsec-

tion P of section 7. That subsection is an exception to the general law of the country, that is to say, it authorizes the acquisition by this company, which was created in 1894, of [DOT]hares in the capital stock of other companies. That was in direct opposition of section 41 of the Companies' Clauses Act of 1891, which provides :
No company shall use any of its funds in the purchase of stock in any other corporation, unless in so far as such purchase is speciallv authorized by the special Act, and also by the Act creating such other corporation.
That is to say, in 1894, this company was given special power, as against the general law of the country, to acquire this stock. That power is not being given now ; it was given in 1894. And moreover, it was given subject to this very unusual provision, that the consideration for the acquiring of that stock might be goods, wares or merchandise sold to the other companies in the ordinary course of business. The general law provided that stock was not to be acquired, but, where exceptions had been allowed, it had been the rule to provide that stock of one company acquired by another should be paid for in cash. So, this was a departure from two principles of the law : In the first place, it gave power to the company to acquire stock in other companies, and, in the second place it allowed the company to acquire such stock without paying cash for it, but by paying in goods, wares and merchandise. If there was any violation of principle, if there was any departure from principle, that violation and that departure took place at that time. Without referring to a previous debate, I may say that every one in this House will remember the acrimonious discussion that occurred when, a few nights ago, we considered a similar clause of the Grand Trunk Pacific, where we provided that the capital stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific might be acquired by the Grand Trunk without paying cash. Why, hon. gentlemen even moved an amendment, declaring that, if tfie stock was acquired, it should be paid for in cash, and they based their argument in support of that amendment on the estimate that this was the general principle of the law. So, which legislation will these hon. gentlemen stand upon ? Do they wish the general law made applicable to this corporation, or do they wish an exception made in the case of this corporation ? I do not know anything about contracts that the company may have with the corporation of the city of Ottawa. I am not concerned with that. I do not know anything about the details of this matter. But let us look at the legislation and see what would be the effect of it, if adopted. It will give this company the same powers that are given to any company incorporated under the Joint Stock Companies' Act of Ontario- no more nor no less. We are told that it will lead to monopoly. But, if so, why does it
not lead to monopoly in all these other cases in Ontario ?
Will the hon. minister allow me to ask him a question ? Are the circumstances in other cases exactly identical with those in the city of Ottawa ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether they are or not. I am simply asking why the argument that is applicable to other companies in Ontario is not applicable to this.

The circumstances, as the hon. minister (Mr. Fitzpatrick) knows are peculiar-unique. Nobody knows that better than the hon. minister himself. Will the hon. minister state, will he endorse the opi-ion of the Minister of Inland Revenue, that this company will be bound by the maximum rate fixed in the agreement made between the city of Ottawa and the Consumers' Electric Company ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know nothing of that contract the hon. gentleman speaks about, nor ami aware that there is anything unique in the position of the city of Ottawa. I have had the pleasure of living here for seven or eight years, and it is an ordinary town, governed in the ordinary way. I do not know that there is anything unique about it.

Is there not this unique about the situation so far as lighting is concerned, that in the contract read by the hon. minister's colleague this afternon, made I think in 1894, between the electric companies that were then consolidated and the city of Ottawa the maximum price was fixed for each electric light ? That since then a contract has been made with another company, and that the maximum price fixed by that contract is much lower than in the previous one ? If that is the case now and if by this legislation we are giving facilities for an amalgamation, the amalgamated company may charge the maximum price, that is the rate fixed in the contract of 1894, which is much higher than that fixed subsequently. The Minister of Inland Revenue, a gentleman well versed in law, has expressed the opinion that if these companies do amalgamate the consolidated company will be bound to charge no more than the maximum rate fixed in the agreement between the city and the Consumers' Light Company. If the Minister of Justice agrees with that opinion, then we can rely upon it.

The Minister of Justice lays down a principle of law which I never heard of before, that is, that a corporation cannot acquire the stock of any other corporation under the General Act unless for cash.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will read the law for my hon. friend. Section 41 of the Companies' Clauses Act, chapter 118 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, says :

No company shall use any of its funds in the purchase of stock in any other corporation, unless in so far as such purchase is specially authorized by the special Act, and also by the Act creating such other corporations.
My hon. friend will see there is no doubt about it. That has been the law since 1867, before I came to the bar.

I am not yet convinced that a corporation cannot pay for anything except in cash where it it authorized to purchase, either by its own Act or by the General Act, and that when it buys shares in any other company it must pay cash.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The first point is as to whether a corporation can acquire the stock in any corporation unless it is authorized by a special Act. I think that point is settled by the section I have read. The other principle of law will be found in section 30 and the preceding sections of the . same Act:
Every shareholder shall, until the whole amount of his stock has been paid up, be individually liable to the creditors of the company to an amount equal to that not paid up thereon.
He has got to pay whatever he is called upon to pay in the first instance-in default of a special arrangement it is 10 per cent- he has got to pay that, and then the shareholder is individually liable to the extent of every farthing that is due on the balance. That is the general principle, that the stock must be paid for in cash. As I said a moment ago, there has been a departure from that.

We are still at loggerheads. I know well that where a party subscribes for stock in a company he Is obliged to pay for it in cash. But my question relates to a case where a company is authorized to purchase stock in another company, that has already been paid for, perhaps. Can they make an arrangement to pay other than by cash ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No doubt they can make an arrangement, no question about that. But the point now is what the general provision of the law- is. As I have shown, the stock must be paid for in cash. Then there may be a departure from that principle, that is, there may be a private arrangement between the twro companies, and if you are dealing with an Ontario corporation the Ontario Act makes special provision for such an agreement But you must have an agreement, and it can only be for certain considerations mentioned in the Act, and that agreement must be deposited with the provincial secretary or the Secretary of State. But that is not the case here. In the absence of subsection (d) of section 7,
[DOT] the section we are now concerned with, this Ottawa Electric Company could not acquire stock in the other company at all. The power, the authority to take stock is con-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
ferred upon them by this section. Now that same subsection would confer upon them the authority to take this stock in a kindred company, that is, a company having kindred purposes. The Act determines the conditions under which they can do it. It was you can take that stock in this kindred company provided you pay for it in goods, wares or merchandise. Now the effect of this amendment is merely to substitute the consideration that is to be paid, that is, cash instead of goods, wares or merchandise.
Now- my hon. friend argues that if that amendment is adopted it w-ill lead to all manner of abuses. I really cannot follow my hon. friend. I have no desire to support a monopoly, although this Act provided for a monopoly, this Act has a monopoly in contemplation. Section 8 of the Act of Incorporation of the Ottawa Electric Company provides for a monopoly of that company.
Read it, please.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is too fast for me. I have no desire to provide for a monopoly, or to be a party to any legislation which w-ill have that effect. Will my hon. friend say that if you authorize this company to take that stock for cash instead of taking it for a consideration to be paid in goods, wares or merchandise, these terrible results will follow ? I cannot see it. If they get it for goods, wares or merchandise, or if they can get it for cash, in what respect will the results differ ? How can these terrible results follow in one case and not in the other ? If they follow at all, they must follow fr6m the fact that this company will acquire the stock. Now how can the result be affected by the manner of payment ? It seems to me that is elementary. l^he hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) and myself may differ In law occasionally, but I have confidence in his business judgment, and I would like him to follow out that point and to show me how the result is to be affected by the consider- ' ation to be paid for that stock. I said a moment ago that this Act of incorporation has a monqpOly in contemplation. Look at section 8 and see what is provided for there. There were three companies in existence when this Act of incorporation was passed ; these three companies were the Standard, the Chaudiere and the Ottawa, the latter having been brought into existence at that time. Section 8 provides :
The directors of the company may, for and in the name of the company, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire and take over in whole or in part, upon such terms as may be agreed upon with the other companies hereinafter mentioned respectively, and may thereafter hold, exercise and enjoy the business, franchises, undertakings, property, rights, powers, privileges, and assets or any of them of the Ottawa Electric Light Company, hereinafter called ' The Ottawa Company,' of the Standard Electric Co. of Ottawa (Limited), and of the Chaudl6re Electric Light and Power Company.

That is to say, it provides specifically for the taking over by this new company of the franchises of the other companies that were then in existence. Now, what is my object in referring to that ? My object in referring to that is to show how my hon. friend from Lincoln has missed the point in referring to the proviso of the'Act. He did not refer to the enacting part which provides the conditions under which they could take over these companies. He simply referred to the proviso.
