I have a good deal of respect for the opinion of the Minister of Justice, and so I would like him to reconsider some of the points he made in connection with this Bill. The Minister of Justice referred to the original Ottawa Electric Company Act of 1894. subsection ' E ' section 7, which allows the company to acquire shares of capital stock of other companies as consideration for goods, wares, or merchandise, sold to other companies in the ordinary course of business ; and he held that that was a special privilege, and that the amendment that was now being asked for would practically restrict the company to buying that stock for cash. However, in answer to the hon. member for South Lanark, the Minister of Justice admitted that If the power were given to the Ottawa Electric Company to acquire shares in other companies without limitation, they would not be confined to payment in cash, but could exercise the privilege which they

have under their original charter. As a consequence, the amendment that is now being asked for, would very greatly extend the privilege of the Ottawa Electric Company in buying shares in other companies, as I think the Minister of Justice will on consideration, admit. It is plain, from the original Act of 1894, that the company is not simply constituted for the purposes of providing light, heat, and power for consumers, but that they can manufacture electrical appliances, and can undertake contracts to equip electric lighting and heating companies, so that it is under section 7 in which they are given the power to manufacture these articles, that they have the right to acquire shares in other companies for the purpose of paying the accounts that have been acquired through their supplying appliances to those other companies. This authority of the Ottawa Electric Company under this original charter can only be exercised to any appreciable extent, in the case of new companies of which they would be practically the promoters. That power has been given to a number of manufacturing corporations, both by the Ontario and the Dominion statutes, and except under the most extraordinary conditions it cannot lead to the merger of the Ottawa Electric Company with the old companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does it permit the acquisition of stock ; that is the question ?
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon; that is not the question. The question is : what is the danger of a merger 7

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not discussing a merger.

I am. I have no objection to this Act whatever, if it does not lead to a merger, and to the formation of a trust. I am quite willing to see the Ottawa Electric Company prosper and grow, so long as it does not grow at the expense of the people. No old established company would need to purchase goods, wares, or merchandise sufficient to enable the Ottawa Electric Company to control an interest in it, but if this Act passes, the Ottawa Electric Company can acquire shares in any company just the same as any private individual can, and by means of their borrowing powers and without pledging their personal credit, by a vote of a majority of the shareholders, they can buy a controlling interest in several existing companies from private shareholders. The hon. minister of Justice said that during the recent debate, members on this side of the House had been insisting that cash should be paid , for the Grand Trunk Pacific stock. I do not think that case is analagous to this, but suppose it were; the fact remains that in the case of one railway company Mr. LAVELL.
buying the stock of another, the public^ is more or less protected by the law which says, that railway rates shall be regulated by a railway commission, whereas in the case of rates charged for electric lighting, and power, there is no statutory limitation on them.	.
I am not one of those who say that a monopoly is always wrong. I can see many cases, especially in the handling of public franchises, where a monopoly might be in the public' interest provided it was kept under public control and operated under proper conditions. In the case of railways for instance we at least have some attempt made to regulate their powers and rates, but there is no provision of that kind in the case of such a company as the Ottawa Electric Company. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) cited the Ontario Act and said that under the Companies Act of Ontario an opportunity was given to all companies to-do exactly what this company asks the privilege of doing. We are not responsible for Ontario legislation and there are many things in the Ontario statutes that will be changed as the people of Ontario grow wiser, but even on this particular point they were wiser in Ontario than this House would be if it passed this Act, for the Ontario House does not permit a company to buy shares in another company except by at least a two-third vote at a general meeting called under special conditions. The Ontario Act goes I think, a little farther than it should go in the public interest, but it does not go anything like as far as this Act will go if we amend it as now proposed and permit the shareholders to buy up the shares of any other companies by a bare majority, something the Ontario Act does not permit. The Ontario Act at least applies to all companies and puts them on an equal basis. If one company has the right to do it, so has every other, but if we read the Acts incorporating these companies, we will see that not one of the existing electric companies of Ottawa has that power now, and if we grant this power to the Ottawa Electric Company it will have the sole right to do these things. In other words it will have a special power and not the general power that will be given to a company incorporated under the Ontario statutes. If the government chooses to take the responsibility of creating this opportunity for forming a monopoly, why does it not take courage and suggest an amendment to the general Act 7 I do not believe it would go further than the Ontario Act; I cannot believe this House would go as far as this Act. It is admitted all over the world by students of legislation that a clause such as this allowing a company unlimited power to buy shares in other and rival companies is the strongest possible basis for the formation of a gigantic trust. We are not bound to follow precedents but every one who has been before the committees knows how strongly

precedents are urged and that if we pass this Bill in its present form we are simply paring the way for all companies that choose to ask for it to obtain similar powers and to be enabled to gobble each other until a series of trusts shall be created in towns where rival companies exist. Tile Minister of Justice said that this Act in its present form created a monopoly. As I read it it certainly did but it created a monopoly after full notice to all who are interested. It stated the companies it was intended .to buy and made special provision in the charter creating that monopoly that no change was to be made in the existing rates. But this Act gives the company power to buy up rival companies without notice to parliament or discussion by the parties interested. We are giving them that right with absolutely no provision for the defence of tne public. In this particular case I have no interest personally beyond the responsibility which every member must assume for all legislation. This is special legislation that would be cited as a precedent and as giving one company a power which none of its rivals have. If it is right to put in this clause it should be brought up in a general way and should be introduced as an amendment to the Companies Act.

Why should we interfere with the Act as it now exists ? The present Act prevents a monopoly in the city of Ottawa. The Ottawa Electric Company is permitted to buy shares but only under such conditions that they cannot under any circumstances buy out existing companies. If the amendment is carried this company will have unique powers such as no other company has unless it receives them by special Act of parliament. This large city enjoys competition in the important matter of electric light and power, and it has been shown that by this amendment the citizens might have to pay an additional $250,000 or $300,000. If they acquired these powers the company might charge 75 cents per 100 amperes. The first duty of this parliament is to protect the rights of the people. Today we have three members of the government rising in their places to defend this Bill and apparently they are the only ones to defend it. Nineteen members voted for it in committee and I have been wondering why some of these men who voted for it do not rise and give some good reason why this amendment should be made. The only reasons we have heard have been advanced by the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Brodeur) who said that an agreement between the city of Ottawa and this company had been broken ; that the city of Ottawa is to-day breaking faith and is not carrying out its contract, but the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue has failed to show in what respect it is breaking faith. Neither he nor any one else has shown one single particular in which the city 136

is not keeping to its agreement. It has not been shown that the city of Ottawa agreed to take any quantity of light, heat or power for either an unlimited or limited space of time. All that is shown is that the city allowed this company the use of its streets for the manufacture and sale to the people of light, heat and power, in consideration ot which the company agrees not to charge more, than 75 cents per 100 amperes, so that the only argument really which has been advanced does not hold good. What argument can be advanced ? A great many members, including myself, are not on the Committee on Private Bills, and have not heard a single reason why this Act on out statutes should be amended as proposed. Why, then, should not the Bill be referred back to the committee, where it may be further discussed and further light thrown upon it 7 The only other argument, namely, that, we should not interfere with the rights of the company to buy ithe stock of other companies, is invalid, if the lawyers are correct in saying that the general law of the country does not allow one company to buy the stock of another. If that be not the law, and if there are many special Acts for the purpose of enabling one company to buy stock in another, I submit that that is an abuse of our power to 'legislate. I submit that we ought to go rather in the other direction, and on every occasion safeguard the rights of the people by providing that when a corporation secures a charter from this House it should not be allowed to buy stock in another company and thus make a merger or trust. Here is a case in which such a provision exists, and we are asked to abrogate the clause which prevents .the creation of a monopoly. I submit no good reason has been given why we should pass the measure, and therefore it ought to be referred back to the committee.

A few words in reply to the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and in support of that of my hon. friend from North Leeds. One would judge, from the argument of the Minister of Justice, that this Bill is a limitation of the powers which are at present enjoyed by the Ottawa Electric Company. Clause 7 of that company's charter gives it the power to :
Acquire stock in the capital stock, debentures and securities of other electric companies or of the companies possessing powers similar to those of the company, as the consideration for goods, wares or merchandise sold to such other companies in the ordinary course of business.
The argument of the Minister of Justice is that this is a power which is in excess of what ought to be given any company, and that the Act amending it is a limitation of that. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Lavell) has struck the right key. He says that this clause enables the parent company, which manufactures all these things, to come to the aid of a subsidiary company toy taking

stock in payment, but the amendment will give the Ottawa Electric Company the right to control the franchise of any other company by purchasing the majority of its stock. It is a good deal worse to give that power to a company than simply to give it the power to acquire stock in exchange for materials furnished. Then there is a question whether, when one company amalgamates with another, it does not assume all the liabilities. If there is an agreement by which this company, which the Ottawa Electric Company intends to purchase, is bound to furnish the [DOT]city with light at a certain price, I have always contended that a merger of the two *companies makes the company which absorbs the other subject to all of the obligations of the company it absorbs. Therefore, if the Ottawa Electric Company should purchase the other, it would be obliged to fur nish light to the city at the same rate. But this Bill will give the Ottawa Company the power to purchase a majority of the stock of the other, and is a great extension of its powers. It gives it the power of purchasing, not only for cash, but under any other arrangement it might make with the stockholders, the shares in the company it desires to control, and the Ottawa Electric Company will become the one which will deal with the city and the consumers. The other company may be kept in existence by the election of a directorate and a president once a year and do no other business. The Bill -simply enables the Ottawa Electric Company to obtain control of this other company which has an agreement with the city of Ottawa to furnish light at nearly half the rates charged by the Ottawa Company. The other company may then go on existing in form and doing nothing, and the Ottawa Company be able to dictate its own terms.

Sir. Speaker, I beg leave to move, seconded by Mr. Hackett, the amendment of which i gave notice :
That the said Bill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills, with instructions to that Committee to add a clause, providing that the power to acquire shares in the capital stock, debentures, or securities of other electric companies shall not apply to the capital pmck, debentures or securities of the Consumers Electric Company, or of the Metropolitan Light and Power Company, or their assigns.
It would seem to me that the case made out here by the hon. senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) would be sufficient in itself to justify this House in returning this Bill to the Private Bills Committee. That hon. gentleman was not at the meeting of the committee when this Bill was considered. He has put before the House to-day a petition of the council of Ottawa, he has submitted numerous arguments, and, altogether, it seems to me, has made out a case that, at least, the members of the House should be willing to investigate, and, for that purpose to send the Bill back to the committee. I had given notice of this amendment before I knew what position the hon. senior member for Ottawa would take on this Bill. I gave notice of this amendment because I was in the Private Bills Committee when the matter was discussed and at that time decided, and I move that amendment now because, I believe, it is but a simple act of justice to the citizens of Ottawa that we should reserve this condition as a safeguard to them against monopoly in light, heat and power in this city. And I think it shoidd go back to the committee

because I believe that in the general confusion that existed in the committee at the time this Bill was considered and passed the members did not fully appreciate the strengthening of monopoly that it involved. The amendment that was put in your hands, Mr. Speaker, is acceptable I understand to the city council of Ottawa, to its mayor and to its solicitor. It is also accepted by the officers of the Canadian Union of. Municipalities. This organization has become a power in this land, and it has taken a part in the contest for the reason that it is opposed to the encroachment of corporations on civic rights in Canada. They came forward of their own volition to oppose this Bill, they came forward to uphold the corporation of the city of Ottawa in resisting the demands that are being made by the Ottawa Electric Light Company at this time. I wish to point out that even if we throw this Bill out altogether we take nothing at all away from the Ottawa Electric Company. We are not threatening their rights or their powers. If at this time they are asking for something improper, asking for something they have no business to get under their contract with the city of Ottawa, then it is certainly our duty to see that this Bill does not become law, and that no powers are given to them which the city of Ottawa are opposed to.
During the afternoon the position of this company and of the other companies named in the amendment have been set forth clearly, and it is not necessary for me to go into that matter more than to say that the Ottawa Electric Company now promoting this Bill is itself an amalgamation of three companies. It has itself a Bill of incorporation that was granted by this parliament, but it was granted as the basis of an agreement between itself and the city of Ottawa. Under the operation of that Act the price of electric power and of light and heat in the city was not to be above a certain fixed maximum. In 1901 the Consumers' Company was incorporated. It started business with a maximum schedule as agreed upon by the city of 52 cents per 100 ampere hours against 75 cents being charged by the Ottawa Company as the maximum rate. As a matter of fact the competition has set a price, not at 52 cents per 100, but at 36 cents per 100. Both the Consumers' and the Ottawa Company are at this time charging that rate, and the people of Ottawa are getting their light and power at that rate. That has been the result, and it seems to me it has justified the action of the city of Ottawa in trying to escape a monopoly in this line of business. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the question of public ownership is not involved in this matter that we have before us to-day. It is merely a matter of lighting the city of Ottawa that is in dispute. The matter we are dealing With relates wholly to the price the citizens of Ottawa will have to pay for their electric light, 1364
heat and energy. That is a different question altogether from public ownership. It the city went into the business of producing electric light and heat, it would be a question of municipal trading in contradistinction to municipal ownership. Bo it seems to me it is out of th'e way altogether to introduce into this discussion the question of municipal ownership. It is purely and distinctiy so far as I can see, a matter of municipal monopoly, of a monopoly in opposition to the interests of the city and the citzens.
I think I would be justified in saying that the inference to be drawn from the Bill before us is that it is the wish of the Ottawa Electric Company to have a monopoly of their business in this city. I say that is a legitimate inference. In the Private Bills Committee that inference was directly contradicted by the representative of the Ottawa Electric Company. I asked him wrhy they had this Bill before the House if that was not their object, and it was explained to the committee that the reason was thi^, that in the near future there was to be a considerable proposition put before the capitalists of this district, including and embracing the acquisition of some large water powers around the Chaudi6re, and that the Ottawa Electric Company expected to be included in this proposition, and therefore they -wanted power to go in and buy up some other water powers, buy out some other companies who have control of water powers just above the Cliaudifire Falls. I accepted that explanation, and put this proposition to the representative of the company : On your own ground, if that is why you are asking for this Bill, then, seeing that the city of Ottawa draws another inference from it, draws the inference that you want a monopoly, in order to meet their objection, will you accept a provision that you shall not invest in any stock or securities of the Metropolitan or Consumers' Company ? If that statement made by them was fair, If it was right, if it was the -whole case, then the proposition I made to them would have been accepted. If that is then-position to-day, then the acceptance of the amendment I am offering does not hurt the Ottawa Electric people at all, does not in any way hamper their movements, and will not interfere with them in carrying out the amalgamation that they expect to make next year in connection with the water powers at the Chaudiere. But, Mr. Speaker, the representative of the company refused to accept this amendment, he refused on this one ground : He said that the company objected on principle to being singled out and being forbidden to invest in the securities of these two other companies. Now I do not think that the representative of the company is the one to bother about the principle, it is for us to look after that principle. It seemed to me then that he was throwing doubts on his own frankness in stating, when this Bill was asked for, that

he objected on principle to having the other two companies exempted from the operation of the Bill. Mr. Speaker, I am led to the conviction by the arguments and facts that were put before the committee, both by the representative of the company, by the mayor and council of Ottawa and by the representations of the Canadian Union of Municipalities. I was forced to the conclusion, as I say, that the whole object of this Bill, innocent though it looks to be, is to give the Ottawa Electric Company a monopoly of the business of supplying light, heat and electric energy to the citizens of Ottawa, so that it may be able, if it thinks proper, to raise its rates up to the full maximum that is granted them under their charter. It is for that reason, and especially since it is being supported by the hon. mem-mer for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) that X ask by my amendment that this Bill be referred back to the Private Bills Committee that we may have the whole matter threshed out there.

That a Select Committee of eleven members of this House be appointed to prepare and introduce a Bill to consolidate and amend-the Acts respecting the public revenue, the control and administration of public moneys, the raising of loans authorized by parliament, and the auditing of the public accounts, with power to send for persons, papers and records and that the right honourable the leader of the government be authorized and requested to name the members of the said committee.
He said. Mr. Speaker, I regret that, dealing with this important subject, I have to begin the discussion at this late hour of the night. But, as there might not be another opportunity for dealing with it, I think it advisable to discuss it, even though I must necessarily do so at some disadvantage, speaking to a House wearied by a long day's work. In calling the attention of the government to a question of the amendment and consolidation of the Revenue and Audit Acts, I feel that I am directing their attention to a subject of importance ; and I hope to be able to give such information to the House or bring such matters to the attention of the House as will probably convince the government that there is immediate necessity of doing something in the line of improving the Audit Act, which has now been in force for over a quarter of a century. The hon. gentleman will recollect that the Audit Act is the creation of a Liberal government. It was introduced by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Right Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) as a member of the Mr. EMMERSON.
Mackenzie government in 1878. And on the 1st of August of that year the present occupant of the position of Auditor General began the duties of his office. Of course, it was, to some extent an experiment; it was a copy of an experiment, because, in 1866, the English parliament had adopted an Act of which ours was largely a copy. We have, therefore, not only an Act that has been in force in this country for twenty-five years, but we have practically an Act that has been in force for forty years. An Act not originating in our own country, but a copy of the English Act, for which reason * also we might anticipate that the time has arrived when some amendment may be required. It is true that our system of government is similar to the British .system, but our conditions are dissimilar. This affords another reason why it may be time to take stock of the situation and see whether, after the time that has elapsed since this Act came into force, and the great development that has taken place in the meantime, it may not be proper for the government now seriously to consider and amend the Act.
In 1878, when this Act was introduced, our total expenditure was, in round numbers, $30,000,000 ; in 1903 our total expenditure has doubled, and is upwards of $60,000,000. We had, from 1874 to 1878, an average expenditure of upwards of $32,000,000, and when this Act was introduced by the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) he considered that the question of the amount of the expenditure was important in the consideration of what precautions we had to take in reference to the audit of the moneys of the country. Some hon. member then remarked to the present Minister of Trade and Commerce : Why, in your time there was no audit at all. He said : We did not need an auditor, because then our expenditure was $14,000,000 less than it is now

in 1878. It was not $14,000,000 less, it was $10,000,000 less, but a matter of $4,000,000 or so, in speaking of the finances of the country, was not very wide of the mark for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In 1878, at all events, all parties were united in the opinion that in view of the existing condition of things, with an annual expenditure of $30,000,000, it was necessary to have a strict Audit Act. If it were necessary then, and the question of the revenue was important, surely it is exceedingly important that now, with our present enormous expenditure and with the possibility of greatly increased expenditure in the near future, by reason of the construction of a national transcontinental railway, when we will be handling money upon a scale that has never existed in Canada before-it is important, I say, that we should to-day see to it that in every way the control of the finances of the country is as it should be. The object of an Audit Act in 1S78. so far as I can gather from the

speeches made a perusal of the Act itself, was that we should have a financial policy controlled by parliament, and that we should have a financial executive administration absolutely controlled by a servant of parliament. Up to that time we had a combination of the Finance Department and the Audit Department, and it was found that that system did nof work satisfactorily. The audit, in fact, was under the control of the Finance Minister. When this Act was introduced in 1S78 the hon. gentleman who introduced it promised a complete separation to all intents and purposes of the position and duties of the Finance Minister and the Auditor General. He promised that so far as it was necessary to maintain an independent audit, we should have an independent auditor. Time went on. Only a short time after the present Auditor General took the position there was a change of government. But matters progressed fairly well, and we found this fortunate state of things, that for many years the Auditor General had the confidence of both parties in parliament and the support of both parties. I am not intimating that the Auditor General has not, to a large extent, the same support yet, except when it comes to matters which affect the financial management of the affairs of the country. The experience df the last few years has shown that complete harmony in that regard does not exist. In 1896 we had the judgment of the hon. gentlemen who at present control the affairs of Canada as to the importance of the duties of the Auditor General, the great value of his services to the country, and the desirability of raising his salary to $4,200, as expressed toy the gentleman who' originally introduced the Act, namely, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Now, the Auditor General has been and was intended to be more than a mere auditor, something more than an officer who could cast up accounts and see that the additions were correct. He was intended to be a controller as well, a check upon the executive administration of the government in respect to finances. This was made abundantly clear by the gentleman who introduced the Act and by those who supported it at the time, and it is also clear by the wording of sections 32 and 33 of the Audit Act in particular, and other sections as well. In 1880 it was found ad visable to enlarge the duties of the Auditor General, and Mr. Kirkpatrick moved a resolution accordingly. In 1888 an increase of salary was voted to the Auditor General, amounting then to $4,000. Several hon. gentlemen then prominent in the House-Mr. Edgar, Mr. Mills, Mr. Weldon, Mr. Casey and the right hon. gentleman who leads the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier)-were very emphatic in the declaration of the importance of sustaining the Auditor General and preserving his functions entirely distinct from the control of the administration, of making
him emphatically an officer of parliament, and of giving him that control over the finances of the country which would practically do away with the possibility of any improper expenditure of money on the part of the executive administration. In 1895 the Hon. Mr. Mills introduced a petition asking that the decision of the Minister of Finance should practically be revoked in favour of the Auditor General, and that notwithstanding that the Minister of Finance had determined that lie could not at that time afford it, the promotions suggested by the Auditor General, this ought to be ordered.
It seemed to be the opinion of Mr. Mills and those who supported him then that not only should the Auditor General be gen-eraljy sustained but that his suggestions should practically override the views of the Minister of Finance as regards a question of policy. In 1896, and that will end the matters of review I have taken the opportunity of referring to, we had the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce again emphasizing the important duties discharged by the Auditor General and suggesting that so valuable had his services become that it was deemed expedient to have the present Senator McMullen read to the House from cover to cover both volumes of the Auditor General's report. Now, this appears to indicate very clearly the views of both the great parliamentary parties as to the functions and duties of the Auditor General and the importance of sustaining his hands and of giving him large powers not only in the interests of the country but of whatever political party may be in power. The more fully the Auditor General is enabled to carry out his views in regard to a careful and prudent executive administration of the moneys of the country the more fully can the government in the end be endorsed by the people who are scrutinizing their acts. I therefore approach this question, as far as a party man can approach a question of this kind, with an honest desire not to make it unnecessarily or unduly a party question. I recognize that in dealing with a matter of this kind I must refer to instances which go to show the necessity for a change and I will naturally refer to instances which are somewhat modern. In doing so I will come to deal with what appears to show the errors of the present administration rather than the errors of the preceding party. But, I am in this singularly happy position that whereas we do not like the tu quoque argument as a rule I will be delighted to have hon. gentlemen opposite instance the delinquencies on the part of those who preceded them of the former administration because the greater the number of instances that are shown of failure to carry out the intention of the Act the more effectually have I placed my case for the consideration of the government. For if I instanced failures of the Act in regard to the present government

alone and there were none during the period when the party I support were in power, it might be said that these were owing alto gether to the gentlemen who are now in power. I do not think that will be found to be the case, but I think on the other hand I can safely leave in the main instances that appertain to the former administration in the hands of the mambers of the government and their supporters. Now, are we still of the same opinion as we were in 1878 and down to 1896, as to the paramount importance of having an officer, who, on behalf of parliament and the people shall check and restrain the financial administration-I should say the executive financial administration-as distinguished from the financial policy of the government ? I have said that for many years the system worked fairly well. I say now advisedly, and I do not do so at all offensively, that it is practically a dead letter. I say in mitigation o' that that it could hardly be otherwise. The Act carried in it the germs of its own failure and when we get an Act of that kind which has stamped upon its face or engraved on its sections, the elements which go to make it unsuccessful, the more time advances, the longer it is in operation, necessarily there will grow up a greater number of precedents and exceptions to its rule so that in the process of time it will be practically a dead letter as it is to-day. Now, I say it could not work' satisfactorily because there are certain exceptions which appear to the main sections giving the Auditor General a semblance of power, but which still leave in effect the whole difficulty which the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke when he introduced the Bill. We have not done away with the controlling power of the Finance Minister ; we have not separated the Finance Minister from the Auditor General and in the present administration the Finance Minister is still king. I will refer as to this to section 32 :
No cheque for public money shall Issue except upon the certificate of the Auditor General that there is parliamentary authority for the expenditure, save only in the following cases :-
(a.) If, upon any application for a cheque, the Auditor General has reported that there is no parliamentary authority for issuing it. then upon the written opinion of the Attorney General of Canada, that there is such authority, citing it, the Minister of Finance and Receiver General may authorize the Deputy Minister of Finance and Receiver General to prepare the cheque, irrespective of the Auditor General's Report.
By that subsection of section 32 alone, I submit that we failed very significantly to carry out what was supposed to be the object of the Bill. Mr. Mitchell said on the occasion of the introduction of this Bill:
This Bill gives us another Governor.
Meaning the Auditor General. But, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said :

No, it gives the Minister of Finance and not the House a Governor, I am inclined to think.
If that had been the effect of the Act-I would not say a governor of the Finance Minister-but I say that If the effect of the Act had been as anticipated by the right hon. gentleman who introduced it so many difficulties as we havp to point out would not have arisen. Clause B provides for emergencies, and I am not disposed to quarrel about that clause. Clause 0 dealing with the Treasury Board, worded as it was, was almost necessarily a fatal blow to the efficient carrying out of the Act. Many difficulties have arisen under that clause and under the following section 33. These difficulties were anticipated by Sir Charles Tupper when the Act was first introduced, and time has proven that he was right. Mr. Tupper said :
The difficulty that appears to present itself to my mind is this :	you are preparing to
give the public an independent parliamentary officer, but who is to see before the payment of public money that under the law it is entitled to be paid ? If you leave the government power to override his decision and pay the money, what then is gained by the Act ?
Our Audit Act is to some extent a copy of the English Act. I am aware that there is a movement in England to improve their Act, but even' if there were not, the conditions are so different in Canada, that I am inclined to think that an Act giving the Aud itor General {or comptroller as he is called in England), less power than we would give our officer here, might be effectual in England and not be effectual in Canada. As a rule, politicians occupy a different status in Canada from that which they occupy in England, and I am! afraid we will have to admit that in Canada politicians and governments hang on to their positions more tenaciously than they do in Great Britain. Section 32 of the Act could not be expected to give reasonable satisfaction, because the application for money or for a credit as the case may be never originates with the Auditor General, hut always with the department. It,is the application of the department, or in fact of the government on one hand and the Auditor General on the other hand, it a cheque is refused an appeal is made by the department, and to whom is this appeal made ? Why, it is made to the very gentleman who is prosecuting the appeal. The Treasury Board consists of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Customs, the Minister of Inland Revenue, the Minister of Justice, the Secretary of State and one other member of the Privy Council with the Deputy Minister of Finance as secretary, it is essentially the government on a smaller scale. And it is the minister, who applies for and is refused a cheque, and his associates to whom the appeal is made. The only difference is that the minister who made application for the cheque has 'less direct responsibility than otherwise. He throws upon the shoulders of several the

responsibility which he otherwise would have to assume, and as no reasons are given by the board, and the mere announcement of the decision is all that is of record, he is not personally responsible in the matter. Time has shown that this provision has not worked satisfactorily and more and more from time to time inroads are being made on what was supposed at the time to be an adequate protection for the people. We are now at the stage when we must consider whether wTe are going to practically abandon the theory of a controller in the financial and executive sense as distinguished from the political sense. 'Section 33 has occasioned a good deal of conflict of opinion. My main object in proposing this motion is to secure a committee that will take into consideration and revise the whole general scheme of an Audit Act. Suggestions have been made from various quarters, and more especially by the Auditor General himself, who has very great experience for over a quarter of a century, in the working of the Audit Act. We occupy in this matter the unique position that we cannot to any great extent find precedents in other countries, and so far as I know we could get any very valuable information by making inquiry abroad.
Decided changes in the 32nd and 33rd sections are required and we also require a number of minor changes as pointed out by the Auditor General in a suggested Act that appears to have been prepared in 1889, I do not know at whose instance. The lines of authority as between the Auditor-General and the various departments should be more clearly defined so that there shall not be the uncertainty that has existed in the past as to the duties of those who have the initiation of the disposition of the money and of the Auditor General, who is intended to have, to a large extent, the control of the money. Either amendments along these lines should be made to the Civil Service Act, the Public Works Act'and the Railway Act or the Audit Act should be amended in such a way as to govern these other Acts and avoid constantly arising difficulties. Take for example the question of tender. Tender is a farce to-day in the Dominion of Canada ; it is not even provided that contracts are to be let by tender, much as we discuss that subject when considering the 'estimates. Not only in certain matters affecting the Department of Railways and Canals, and whether tenders are asxed or not, once a contract is let, however outrageous its terms may be, the contention of the departments is that there can toe no inquiry into the prices that are toeing paid. Some twenty-five of the eighty sections of the Act require the consideration either of the government or of a committee.
We want also a more expeditious publication of the Auditor General's Report.
This report ought to be published in sections according to departments ; as rapidly as reports of these departments are prepared they ought to be placed in the hands of the representatives of the people, before they assemble in parliament, so that members can familiarize themselves with their contents and be able to intelligently discuss them in the interests of the people. I am not alone in thinking this. In 1887 parliament met on April 13, and the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) on the 15th insisted upon having the Auditor General's Report then. In 1886, parliament met on Friday, the 19th, and on Monday the present Senator McMullen made a violent statement in reference to the necessity of members of parliament having these books in their hands at an early date, although the time had not arrived according to the statutory requirements. Whatever other changes may be made, I think the decisions of the Treasury Board should be made public in the same way as the Blue-books are distributed. They should be published from time to time and distributed so that the people should know exactly what attitude has been taken in reference to the moneys belonging to the country. The Auditor General suggests that the occupant of the office should be styled the Controller and Auditor General. The corresponding officer in England is so called. The Auditor also advocates a Canadian exchequer account corresponding with the English exchequer account.
In support of the position I have taken it will be necessary for me to refer to some instances in which I think the Act has not worked satisfactorily. The provisions as to tender have failed to accomplish the purpose intended. I understand that it has been said by members of the government that I am seeking to invade the sacred region of responsible government toy the motion that I propose. If that is so it is rather a peculiar departure, because I belong to a party which is not given to that kind of thing. I am not wedded at all to the proposition which I make ; I ask the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who leads the House, by my motion, to name a committee to consider this matter and probably to bring in a Bill amending the Act. It is important that we should have such a Bill. I could have brought in a Bill myself and have submitted it to the House, and the House would then doubtless have entertained it and probably have referred it to a special committee. I do not know that there is any radical departure from the principles of responsible government in asking that a committee of members of the House shall assume the duty of investigating such a matter as this and reporting it to parliament leaving it to parliament in

its wisdom to either accept or reject it. At all events I was guided in the first instance by a reference to rule 39, which says :
Every Bill is introduced upon motion for leave, specifying the title of the Bill ; or upou motion for a committee to prepare and bring it in.
I was guided further by searching the journals of the House and finding instances in which this course had been adopted in the past. Among others I found that in 1879, as recorded on page 63~ and 64 of the Journals of the House, a motion was made by Mr. Macdonald, seconded by Mr. Bowell, that a committee consisting of fifteen members should be appointed to take evidence and send for papers and documents in order to bring in a Bill with reference to the insolvency law. That was subsequently reported to the House. Last year we had the question of the election laws referred to a select committee and we had the committee on the redistribution of seats. I may also cite another authority, which i think will commend itself to both sic.es, and that is the precedent set by the British House of Commons in April, 1893. of appointing a select committee on the question of national expenditure. So that I think I may fairly submit that I am not asking for any radical departure from the principles of responsible government when I ask the House to name a select committee to consider a question which is of such immediate importance. For forty years we have had practically the same Audit Act m force, for our Act is founded on one forty years old. Since then our expenditure has doubled, and there is no doubt that our expenditure will be on a vaster scale during the next ten or twelve years.
Before I refer to the Davis contract I want to say that i hope I shall deal with this question in such a way as not to unnecessarily excite the hostility of the right hon. leader of the government. I should be delighted to stop here and now if the right hon. gentleman would give me an intimation that he will appoint the committee I suggest or any committee. I only name eleven members as a suggestion and I want it to be distinctly understood that I do not consider this a party question. It is one from which we should eliminate politics as far as possible. Coming back to the Davis contract, I wish to refer to a letter which is found upon the first page of the Auditor General's Report, dated at the Auditor General's office, Ottawa, March 9th, 1904.
I have the honour to transmit my report on expenditure accounts, appropriation and statutory, and on revenue accounts, for the fiscal year 1902-3.
The following rather lengthy correspondence is introduced in this place because it illustrates the practical importance of several Mr. LENNOX.
amendments that this office has been asking for some years to have made to the Audit Act.
This refers mainly to the Davis contract and no doubt also to the Corry and Da-verdure contract. I propose therefore to refer to these matters and, as I wrote to the Minister of Railways and Canals the other day, I propose to also refer to the question of the Farran's Point Canal. Mr. McDougall says further.
The magnitude and number of the transactions going through this office are now so increased that I feel parliament should seriously consider also the amendment of the Audit Act along the other lines suggested in a former report, to enable this office to cope with the expansion of the business of the country. I feel so strongly on this point that if parliament does not see its way to bring the matter up this session, I shall at the end of the session ask to be superannuated.
I would like to have brought this matter up earlier, but I was advised not to do so as it would have been overshadowed by the discussion of the transcontinental scheme and would not have attracted the attention it deserves. However, on the 3rd of May I gave notice of the motion which I am moving to-night. Before that, when I had the matter in hand, I referred on the 22nd of April to the matter which I proposed to discuss to-night, in a few sentences which I will take the liberty of reading :
I repeat, and it cannot be too ;mpliatically enunciated, that there is a great constitutional safeguard of the people of Canada at issue in the question we are discussing to-night. If hon. gentlemen who are familiar with the laws and practices of parliament will for one moment reflect, they will see that three great safeguards stand out conspicuously in the constitution of Canada. One concerns the paying o''t of money of the people of Canada. The gieat safeguard in reference to that, which prevents the administration to a large extent, thouth not fully, I am sorry Jo say, from squandering the resources of the people of Canada, was the institution of the Audit Office, and the administration of that office by the present incumbent. Too much -cannot be said of the efficient manner in which that gentleman has administered that office, and of the sturdy ard loyal way in which he has stood up for the rights of the people as against the Acts of the present administration.
In seme instances, in one instance that occurs to mind, into which I shall not go at present, as large a sum as over half a million dollars was saved to the people by the activity and loyalty of this officer. And even then he failed to accomplish all he thought should have been accomplished on behalf of the people. That is one of the safeguards, which stands out conspicuously.
Now, in the controversy that has arisen between the Auditor General and the Treasury Board and the Department of Railways, although the Auditor General was fought at every point, opposed on every issue-and I must say, not very courteously

so far as the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals was concerned-in the end, although the Treasury Board overruled the Auditor General on every contention he advanced, and found that Mr. M. P. Davis was entitled to all that he asked, to all that the contract named, and to all that he had sent in his hill for, including the right to obtain payment in some manner for 79 years to come, yet after all that had been done, the government, for some reason as yet unexplained, saw fit to withdraw their decision, to consult with the Auditor General and get him to agree to a substituted contract, a vast improvement it is true upon the contract which was made in 1900, but which yet does not fully secure the interests of the people of Canada. Now the results of that substituted contract carrying out the reversal of the judgment of the Treasury Board, has been that at least three-quarters of a million dollars have been saved to the people of Canada. It will be necessary for me to read a portion of the memorandum of the Minister of Railways and Canals upon which the Order in Council was made.
On a memorandum dated September 26, 1900, from the Minister of Railways and Canals representing that, in the opinion of the chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals, in which he (the minister) concurs, it is highly desirable that the system of electric lock operation and electric lighting which has been satisfactorily adopted on the Soulanges canal and is about to be adopted on the Lachine canal, should be brought into use on the Cornwall canal, where facilities for the creation of the necessary power already exist.
The minister further represents that under lease, dated June 25, 1896, issued to Mr. Michael P. Davis, the following provisions are inserted :-
I am not reading continuously, I am paraphrasing to some extent.
That the lessee shall apply electric power to the satisfaction of the Chief Engineer of Railways and Canals for the working of all the locks on the Cornwall canal at $63 per horse power per annum ;
That the lessee shall also supply and work electric direct current arc lights of not less than 2,000 candle power, in perfect working order, at such points and in such number as shall from time to time be deemed necessary by the chief engineer aforesaid, running all night wherever so required, along the canal, at the rate of 30 cents a night. The minister recommends that In pursuance of the said lease, provisions, he be authorized to enter into a contract with Mr. M. P. Davis for lighting the Cornwall, canal, the number of lights not to be less than 250 arc lights of 2,000 candle power, or more than 270, at the discretion of the Department of Railways and Canals, to be paid for at 30 cents per lamp for each night during which the light Is required and supplied ; further, for the supply of electric power for the operation of the lock gates and valves, and of bridges throughout the said canal ; the amount to he paid for such service to be $63 per horse power per annum for a minimum of 400 horse power.
The minister says that it is highly desirable that this contract should be entered into. Why it was highly desirable I have been at a loss to ascertain. Was it for economy ? It may have been, but it is pretty hard to make that out. Whatever else "the government have failed in-we all fail more or less-the present administration I suppose have not failed in the matter of economy-rigid economy, I expect those hon. gentlemen on the back benches would say. Rigid economy in'every department of the public service is still the warp and woof of the banner of the Liberal party. They all appear in that. Now, I have read the memorandum of October 9, 1900, that was to adopt the contract for 21 years. We cannot have too much of a good thing, and consequently on October 16, 1900, an Order in Council was made-[DOT]
On a memorandum dated the 15th of October, from the Minister of Railways and Canals, recommending that the Order in Council of October 9 authorizing the entry Into contract with Mr. Davis in respect to the lighting, &c., by electricity of the Cornwall canal, be amended to such effect that the terms of 21 years therein named as the terms of said lease may be extended by successive renewals July 1st, 1979, thereby bringing it into conformity with the lease the water power granted to Mr. Davis mentioned in the said order.
Now, what was our position in November, 1900, at the time when the contract was entered into ? We were paying, for the year which ended on 30th June, 1900, salaries, wages, care and operation of the Cornwall canal $18,181, and we were paying for lighting $342, a total of $18,423. Mr. Davis had a terminable lease. We were receiving $1,000 and we were carrying out a policy which was inaugurated many years ago of giving leases along the canal "for the purpose of developing the power and so encouraging industrial life along the various canals ? The rental, it is true, was not very much,-but the benefit to the country was considerable in that way. Light and energy were available under the contract that existed at that time, in which it is recited that we can take that light from Mr. Davis and can procure electric energy from him if we desired it,-we could take it or not as we preferred. And there had been nothing done under the terms of the contract, so that, if the government had seen lit to terminate the lease in 1900 they could have done so without the sacrifice of a dollar. It was provided in the agreemnt entered into in 189t>:
Provided always that these presents are upon the express understanding that the lessor reserves the right as follows, namely :	If, at
any time hereafter, the land hereby demised and the quantity of surplus water leased or which may hereafter be leased, according to the Intent and meaning thereof or any part thereof, are or Is required for the use of the canal or for any other purpose whatsoever, or if the lessor shall elect to take over any and

all buildings and works or erections constructed upon the land hereby demised or the increased flow of water so passing or ,to pass through the works of the said lessee through Hoople's creek, and to take over any and all works and land through which the said increased flow of water passes, thereupon on reasonable notice (not less than twelve calendar months) being given to the lessee to that effect, this lease or lease for the term then current and all the covenants, privileges and rights of the said lessee shall cease and be void, and the lessor shall pay the then value of all such buildings, lands and works with an addition of five per cent thereto, that may be at that time erected or connected therewith and belonging to the lessee ; and that in default of agreement as to the valuation of such buildings, lands and works, their value shall be ascertained by three arbitrators, one to be chosen by the Minister of Railway and Canals, another by the lessee, and the third by the two arbitrators so chosen, and the award of the said arbitrators or any two of them after hearing the evidence offered by either party shall be conclusive as to such value.
As I say, nothing has been done, no building had been erected and the government were in a position-I am not saying they were bound to do it, but they were in a position if they saw fit-to terminate the lease. It was, as far as I can see-it will to be for the government to give their pronouncement on the matter-a prudent lease. It provided that so much of the surplus water, if any, at lock 30 level at Cornwall canal, as the lessor might deem advisable after navigation and existing mills and mill sites hereafter to be leased shall be supplied, should be granted to and taken by the lessee. It appeared, I say to be a prudent lease. I suppose I need hardly anticipate that the government will say it was not a prudent lease in face of the fact that they afterwards implemented it and put it in operation by fixing prices and entering into the contract to which I will now refer.
It will be necessary for me to read but few clauses of this lease, Let me read first the recital:
An agreement made this nineteenth day of October, one thousand nine hundred, between Her Majesty the Queen represented herein by the Minister of Railways and Canals, acting under the authority of an Order in Council dated the ninth day of October, A.D. 1900, as amended by Order in Council datpd the sixteenth day of October, A.D. 1900, of the first part ;

Davis, of Ottawa, in the county of Carleton, contractor, of the second part ;
Whereas, by indenture No. 12,336, dated twenty-fifth day of June, 1896, made between the parties above named, the said Michael P. Davis among other things agreed-
-to supply certain electric power and also electric light at 30 cents per night per light, as by reference to the indenture will more fully appear. It provided that the said Michael P. Davis should supply such light from 1st May. 1900, and current for power from 1st October, 1901. The agreement, so Mr. LENNOX.
far as the light is concerned, was extended by the deputy Minister of Railways and Canals to 1st August, 1901. It was extended by the acting Minister of Railways, under Order in Council to 1st October, 1901, and it was extended to the l'5th November, 1901, by the Minister of Railways and Canals. It was provided further that nothing herein shall be taken to vary other than as above speci-field or provided any of the provisions of the last indenture. I have read over the clauses which are material tor the purpose of reference later on. Now, it is stated in the minute presented to the Governor in Council that the Soulanges canal had been found to work satisfactorily. This was a case of government ownership and operation. And it is a proper inquiry in this regard to ask why it is that, if the Soulanges canal was working satisfactorily under government control and operation and was costing a comparatively small sum of money, why it was that the government thought it necessary to incur this enormous expense of some 852,000 a year involved in this new contract and more than $52,000 a year when the matter would be in full operation, perhaps-why it was 'that the government thought it necessary to enter into this new contract making necessary this large expenditure of money.
Now, taking the highest estimates of Mr. Munro, the superintending engineer at Co-teau Landing and Mr. Hoffmeister the resident engineer with the electrical company on the Soulanges Canal, the total expenditure for the operation and interest account of the Soulanges Canal would not exceed $11,700 a year. We have made a change and what did we affect by the change ? Instead of paying at the outsidie siome $18,000 a year all told, for the operation of the Cornwall Canal, and I will show that the average operation for the last seven or eight years has not amounted to such a large figure as I have mentioned, we incurred an additional expenditure-not a complete expenditure-of about $52,000. We undertook to take 250 lights every night in the year for 79 years at 30 cents per light per night, wanted or not wanted, used or not used, in contrast with what we were bound to take under the contract entered into in 1896 by which we were to have :
2,000 candle power in perfect working order at such points and in such numbers as is from time to time deemed necesary by the chief engineer aforesaid running all night when required.
In other words, we could take or not take the light just as we liked and we could take just such a quantity as we saw fit. We bound ourselves also to take four hundred horse-power, wanted or not wanted, for the same period of time at $63 per horse-power. This means that for lighting we have 250 x 365 x 30. making $27,275 ; 400 horse-power at the rate of $63

per horse-power, making $25,200, or a total expenditure for these two items of $52,575 a year. Multiply that by the time to which we are committed'. Mind you that this not only committed us to an additional expenditure for the time to come, that this did not begin at the end of the old contract which had 17 years to run, but it took immediate effect and put upon us that additional burden for 79 years which would represent, if you multiply the $52,575 by 79, $4,153,425. I will not say that that is the fair way of looking at it. We have to borrow money from year to year and if we borrow the money certainly it will not be less than $4,000,000. However, I do not propose to look at it in that way. I have the figures taken from the public accounts to show the expense of operating the Cornwall Canal from year to year and I will give the years as terminating with the 30th June in each ease.
