ciples of responsible government and the safeguard of public audit introduced by the Liberals in 1878. Taking the contract of 1900, I have shown that according to its reading, and according to the account presented by Mr. Davis, it amounts to $52,575 a year. That contract has been changed ; and the present contract, made in 1908, after the Auditor General had protested, after he had called the attention of the government to various matters which requiring further consideration, after he had called attention to the fact that there had been no tenders called for, the Deputy Minister of Railways took it upon himself to say that there should not be even a certificate that the price was fair and just according to the concluding words of section 33. Well, after the Treasury Board had overruled all the objections of the Auditor General, then the government decided to retrace their steps, and we have a new contract changed in some particulars from the old. We have a contract by which for 243 nights in the year 250 lights are to be supplied at 30 cents a light making $18,225 if they are supplied. For 122 nights 100 lights are to be charged for at the same price making $3,300 and 125 horse power instead of 400 horse power at $63, making an annual charge of $7,875 or a total outstanding charge so long as the present condition of things remains, of $29,700, a saving to the country of $22,815 a year or taking it at its present cash value for 79 years, counting money at 3 per cent, a saving to the country of three-quarters of a million practically, or at all avents of $084,450. The Auditor General has shown that he investigated the Soulanges canal and found it to be practically the same, corresponding in all essential particulars with the Cornwall canal. He found that it was similar in the matter of light and expenditure and he obtained engineers to investigate it. Their report was presented to the government and I am at a loss to understand, when the total operating expenses of the Soulanges canal is not more than somewhere between $10,000 and $12,0U0 a year including the interest, that we should be justified in paying $30,000 for practically the same work on the Cornwall canal.
Did you say that included interest on the investment ?

That is the way the Auditor General put it and that is the way the engineer put it. That is the way I understood it. If the Auditor General's figures are correct I would not be satisfied with the $30,000 we are paying under the amended arrangement of 1903.
It is surely a strange proceeding to begin the supply of electric current on the 1st of October. It may be that the government will explain that this is perfectly correct. When the government entered into this contract with Mr. Davis and he was to begin [DOT] Mr. LENNOX.
furnishing the light on May 1st,'it appeared to be all right but it seems to me to have been very unfair to allow Mr. Davis under that contract to begin supplying electric energy on October 1st. It seems also unfair that the people of this country should have to begin to pay this large amount of $63 per horse power, at a season when for four or five months at all events we would not require it. Under the original contract light was to be furnished by the first of May but that condition was altered and finally there was an agreement that instead of furnishing it on the 1st of May it should commence to be furnished on November 15th, 1901. That date is significant as I shall point out later on. Mr. Davis, claimed that light and power were furnished on October 24. It was one of the questions in dispute between the department and the Auditor General, whether as a matter of fact light was turned out on October 24. If we were discussing this question to-night from a political stanpoint I should ask the government to explain how it is that on October 26th, two days after the date at which Mr. Davis says he turned on the electric lights, keeping them continuously in operation until the month of April following, we find the hon. the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair) under the authority of an Order in Council, signing an extension of time for the completion of this work until [DOT]November 15th.
At all events until, the loth of November or later, there was not a light supplied by M. T. Davis along the Cornwall canal. I think the conclusion is irresistible. I have not gone into the details of the correspondence and the discussions between the Auditor General and the government, but have simply indicated some of the difficulties existing. Mr. Aylesworth, who was consulted by Mr. McDougall, was of the opinion that the Auditor-General was not legally correct in some of the positions he took. But whether the position which he took was on all points sustainable as matter of law or not, it was a position, in the interests of the country, and upon the merits he justified in taking it. Mr. Aylesworth thought the government was bound by the contract, although no public tender was asked, and although he thought the government should have limited the contract to the number of lights actually in use and the number of horse-power. Having regard, however, to the literal construction of the contract, Mr. Aylesworth thought the government are bound to pay. So far as the argument I am now making is concerned, it does not matter whether they were or not, but let me say that much as I admire Mr. Aylesworth's great ability, 1 am inclined to think that if we look to the initiation of the contract and to the basis upon which it was founded, we cannot come to the conclusion that Mr. Aylesworth is correct in his opinion that the country was bound by the contract entered into in November, 1900. I take this ground,

that when the Minister of Railways, on the 2tith of September, 1900, submitted his memo, to the council, he submitted it too upon the basis of a lease which then was in existence, and which provided that the electric lights should be in perfect working order, to be set at such points and in such numbers as the chief engineer shall deem necessary from time to time, and to run all night whenever required. The minister recommends that he be authorized to enter into a contract with Mr. Davis for the lighting of the canal in pursuance of the lease which then existed, and an Order in Council was made upon the basis of the memo. I have read. Then when the new contract came to be made, it is said that the Minister of Railways and Canals was acting under the authority of the Order in Council dated 9th of October, 1900, as amended by the Order in Council dated 10th October, 1900. And it concluded with those words :
For lighting of the said canal at SO cents per night per light, as by reference io the said indenture will more fully appear, and be it further provided that nothing herein shall be taken to vary, other than as herein specifled or provided any of the provisions of the said indenture.
So that I submit that upon the proper construction of the memo, presented to council and the Order in Council and the contract made in November, 1900, the government never were bound to Mr. Davis, and their proper duty was to have paid him for what he did furnish and put an end to the matter altogether. I do not propose to lay any weight upon the fact that this was entered into on the eve of an election. Politically speaking that may be of significance, but I do not attach any importance to it in the matter with which I am dealing now. I do not attach any great importance to the fact that the Auditor-General claims-whether rightly or wrongly-that at the time this contract was en-! tered into, electric energy was being furnished in Ottawa at $15 per horse power, instead of $63. This matter is not perhaps of great moment in the question I have brought up, but it is all-important that the contract was let without tender at a time when we had upon our statutes a law recuring tenders to be called. I do not think the government will say that by reason of the existing lease, they were preeluded from calling for tenders. That cannot be argued with any degree of force in view of the fact that no work had been done under the arrangement which was entered into in 1896. that it was practically a mere license authorizing Mr. Davis to use the waters of Hoople's creek and get such surplus water ns remained after the government had supplied all that was required for navigation, &c.
137	'

Seeing that there was a complete and perfect right of putting an end to that contract any day they liked, seeing that electrical development which has progressed in such a marvellous way had made considerable strides in the years from 1896 to 1900, and was yet in its infancy, and it was not desirable that the government should commit itself rashly where the possibilities were so great of even more wonderful achievement from year to year resulting in lotver-ing the prices-under all these circumstances-the government will hardly claim that they were handicapped or hindered by the terms of the lease of 1896. However, that remains to be seen. I say it is important then, in view of the evidence we have not only in this matter, but in numerous other matters spread over the pages of the Auditor General's Report of preceding years, that we should take steps not only for the improvement of the Audit Act but also for the improvement of the various Acts under which the government let public contracts not only in reference to railways, where some of the greatest abuses have existed, and of canals which are in harmony with the railways in this respect, but in the matter of public works generally. I think it important also that we should consider very carefully the effect of the provisions, or what were intended to be the provisions of the 33rd section. I barely referred to that before. I want to make only one suggestion before I close-for 1 have decided, mainly out of consideration for hon. gentlemen opposite, but also for myself, not to give to-night the other matters I referred to ; perhaps there will be another opportunity to deal with these. I will confine myself to this operation and the others to which X have referred. I had overlooked, in the course of dealing with this question, the matter I particularly wished to present to the government, and that is-assuming that the government are of opinion that there can be and there ought to be some change in regard to the management of the finances of the country-the need that exists for giving some more effective control to the Auditor General or, if not a more effective control to the Auditor General yet, less power to the Treasury Board which is practically the administration. In case the government are of opinion that it is a matter worth considering. I might suggest that something might he done in the direction of committing some matters of the department to a court, say the Exchequer Court or the Supreme Court, not by way of a trial but by way of a reference. just as if matters were referred to the Treasury Board. I anticipate that I may very well be met with the objection : Surely that is the invasion of constitutional government ; are you going to suggest that we should carry on the administration of the affairs of Canada through a legal tribunal ? It does seem to have a very significant hearing upon the argument. I feel that there
edition

may be some force in the argument, but the matter is for the government to consider. I am not as strong an advocate of judges as I used to be. There was a time when I thought we could wisely commit even the distribution of our seats in this House to the judges. I remember I used to argue that when I was young, up in the country. But I do not think so now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But there is a good time coming.

Well, of course, it goes "without saying that I would rather depend upon the Conservatives in power. But I would infinitely rather depend upon the present administration or any administration, than' upon judges in matters of that kind. But, yet, in this matter, which, probably, does not involve a question of political expediency or policy, which pertains to a matter of detail to a large extent very often involves a very nice question of law, and, as a matter of executive administration, I am not sure at all that that might not be a line which could profitably be pursued. I make the suggestion so that the government may consider the matter ; or, if the matter gets to committee, the committee will have it before them and it will come up for further consideration. Now, I think I am right in assuming from what I have shown that there is a necessity for reconsidering this question. And I am strongly in favour- every man in this House is entitled to his own opinion-of enlarging to some extent the powers of the Auditor General. I am not speaking of the present officer particularly. I have a great deal of faith in him. I have so much faith in him that I would like to see the Auditor General who is in office to-day or any succeeding Auditor General receive a much larger salary than he receives. I think we should give our Auditor General a large salary, and that that salary should command the service of the best man of that class in the country, the class whose minds run in the direction of finances. I am in favour of extending the power of the Auditor General, but more particularly of defining clearly the limits of the powers of the Auditor General and of those with whom he comes in contact and to give to the public ready, prompt, and complete information from time to time of what is transpiring between the government and this official. The more you extend the power of the Auditor General in the hands of a suitable man,-within reasonable limits- the more satisfactory will be the management of the money of the country and the more satisfactory account will the administration be able to present to the people of the country.
I am convinced that many times departmental matters are put through by a department which the government, as a whole, probably would rather had not gone through, Mr. LENNOX.
but the government has to take the responsibility of them as a whole. I believe that the trend is towards the enlargement of the powers of officials standing in this relation to the government. I have inquired in reference to France and Germany, and have not been able to get the information ; and therefore, like the Minister of Justice, 1 won't try to talk about a thing that I know nothing about. In regard to the United States, I have looked over a consolidation of their statutes, and it appears to me that they manage this matter in a way that might be beneficially considered in Canada. I do not think we should take our methods from the United States, but we need not hesitate to look anywhere for suggestions. I understand from reading their statutes that they have six auditors and two comptrollers. The chief controller appears to have a staff of officials, for instance, engineers and architects whom he brings to his service from time to time for the purpose of acquainting him with what is going on, and giving him correct estimates. We might find that unduly expensive in our j case. But the controller of customs also .has the right to say whether an account shall be passed, and he can at any time, within a year after it has been investigated by his subordinates, that is by the auditors, finally determine the matter himself, and this binds the executive department. In addition to that, it appears that after that remedy has been adopted by the controller, it is for the individual who is affected, the contractor, to bring the matter intr>
the courts to have it determined. If the United States is entitled to -a verdict, then the controller is justified, if not, he is overruled by the courts.
I will refer to only one other country which can give us any basis upon which to form an opinion, except such circumstances as exist within our own country. I find that so far as I can judge, the tendency in England is to extend the powers of the Auditor General. I understand from reading occasional reports that the Auditor General seems to have been inclined to extend his powers. In the report of the Select Committee on National Expenditure last yeat'7 1 find on page 4, section 2, this statement :
Under the Exchequer and Audit Act of 1866 this officer (who is completely independent of all departments, including the Treasury, and whose tenure of office is similar to that of a judge), was appointed not only to see that no money was issued without .authomy, hut also to examine on behalf of the House if Commons the accounts of the expenditure of the grants in supply, and to report to parliament.
That is a pretty broad proposition in itself. Absolutely independent of all departments, including the treasury, tenure of office similar to that of a judge, and who is appointed to see that no money is issued without authority. Now if that is to be taken lit-

erally, that no money is to be issued without the authority of the Auditor General, then we need not ask for anything more.
The Comptroller and Auditor General in examination before us sticad that he conceived his functions to go beyond mere audit, and that encouraged by the Public Accounts Committee he entered also into the merits of expenditure.
That is what our Auditor General did upon the occasion to which I have referred.
Your committee consider that this retrospective examination, both by the Comptroller and Auditor General and by the Public Accounts Committee, has been well done, and they recommend the Public Accounts Committee, even more than in the past, to encourage the Comptroller and Auditor General to scrutinize and criticise improper or wasteful expenditure, and to indicate where censure is in his opinion required.
It appears therefore that there is a tendency in England to enlarge rather than to curtail the powers of the Auditor General. Now I desire to read the 33rd section of our Audit Act for the benefit of those persons who may not have access to it. It is of great importance :
No payment shall be authorized by the Auditor General in respect of work performed, or material supplied, by any person in connection with any part of the public service of Canada, unless, in addition to any other voucher or certificate which is required in that behalf, the officer under whose special charge such part of the public service is, certifies that such work has been performed, or such material is supplied as the case may be and that the price charged is according to the contract, or, if not covered by a contract, is fair and just.
This was a matter upon which the late Mr. Mackenzie was more pronounced than upon any other. He foresaw, apparently, the difficulties that have arisen, namely, the conflicting questions that arise in regard to extras, and he intended by this section as it now stands to put an end to the question of extras. He said that he had an invincible repugnance to the word ' extras ', and that he would consent to amend the section, which was then the 34th section as it was proposed, and which was much looser than it is now, and he would consent to have it include, as section 33 does now, a provision that the price charged is according to contract, or, if not covered by contract, then there must be a certificate of the officer in charge that the prices were fair and just.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Though the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) has done me the honour to request me to name the committee which he has proposed to the House, I am sorry to say I do not think I can avail myself of his courtesy nor do I believe that my hon. friend has made out a case for the appointment of such a committee as he contemplates by this motion. My hon. friend's motion states that he wants a committee :
137i
To prepare and introduce a Bill to consolidate and amend the Acts respecting the public revenue, the control and administration of public moneys, the raising of loans authorized by parliament, and the auditing of the public accounts.
I did not observe from the remarks of my hon. friend that he stated anything in regard to the raising of loans authorized by parliament. The speech in which he dealt with the motion was sufficiently comprehensive of itself to perhaps make him leave aside that question which, however, he thought it advisable to introduce in his motion. I cannot see that the hon. gentleman gave us any reason at the present time even to consider what amendment could be devised to the Act which exists to-day for the raising of loans authorized by parliament. Then, I do not remember having heard anything from my hon. friend suggesting the necessity of revising the statutes in regard to the public revenue. I cannot see in that direction what parliament could do more than we have done up to the present time. The levying of the public revenue is controlled by parliament under the direction of the Minister of Finance who delivers his budget speech every year and suggests to the House what is necessary and the sources from which the revenue is to be levied. But, my hon. friend, concentrated his remarks upon the control and administration of the public moneys and upon those points it will be sufficient to follow him. My hon. friend stated that the Audit Act had been on the statute-books since 1878 and that it ought to be revised and amended. The first reason which he gave in favour of amending the Audit Act was that it has existed with very little alteration, if any, since 1878 and that it is now somewhat antiquated. He says that it has been in existence for twenty-six years, or rather, as he said, for nearly forty years since it is a copy of the English Act which has been in existence since 1866. The fact that the Act is forty years old is certainly not of itself a reason why we should endeavour to amend it or think of amending it unless some further and sufficient reason for amending it is presented. My hon. friend stated that the revenue had more than doubled since the Act was put on the statute-book. So it has.
And so has the expenditure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think that this fact militates against the disposition of the Act itself. In so far as I understand the matter I think the principle and details of the Act are quite sufficient to take care of the present revenue and of a revenue much larger. If there were any evidence required of that we would have it in the fact that our Act is copied from the English Act and the English Act has been found sufficient to deal with a revenue ten times greater than our own. It may be true that

the tendency to-day is to enlarge the power of the Auditor General, but it has not been found in practice, and if the tendency is in that direction, a statement which I am not prepared either to affirm or deny, all X have to observe to my hon. friend is that that tendency has not been crystallized into an Act of parliament, so that if it be the tendency there is a contrary disposition to leave his power where they are. Therefore all these reasons have no practical value In my judgment. But, my hon. friend has based the better part of his argument upon sections 32 and 33 of the Act. He thinks that under section 32, subsection (c), of the Act the powers of the Auditor General are not broad enough and that they should be extended. Well, the powers of the Auditor General under section 32 are that if an appropriation is asked for any expenditure it is for him to give his opinion to the government whether this appropriation has been voted by parliament and whether it is an expenditure which ought to be incurred and for which there is authority. When he has done that he has exhausted his authority. His opinion is submitted to the Treasury Board and is passed on by the Treasury Board which is simply a sub-committee of council itself. Oases may arise, as they have arisen more than once during the twenty-six years that the Act has been in operation, where the Auditor General will be of the opinion that an expenditure is not authorized by parliament, that it has not been voted, that it does not come within the purview of the appropriation because all the power that the Auditor General has is to say whether or not the appropriation that is asked from him is authorized by law. When he has done that and when he has come to the conclusion, for instance, as many times it will be the case that the appropriation which is asked by any of the departments of government is not justified or is not authorized, there must be some authority to decide whether he is right or wrong and what authority has to do that ? The only authority in my estimation, and I think it is the only authority in the estimation of my hon. friend, is parliament, which will sit in judgment not only upon the Auditor General but upon the Treasury Board and upon the government. After the opinion of the Auditor General has been given it goes to the Treasury Board and the opinion of the Auditor General may be sanctioned or it may be rejected. If it is sanctioned the matter is ended there. If it is rejected there comes into operation all the check which is intended by parliament not only in this country but in Great Britain ; that is to say that then the Auditor General has power to constitute parliament a court of appeal to decide between him and the government. It is true that the payment may have been made in the meantime and will have been made, but if the payment had not been made in the meantime it might be

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: that, the whole power of the government might be blocked, it might be that the whole administration of the government might be blocked, and therefore it has been thought proper in the judgment of the British parliament, as it has been thought proper also in the judgment of the Canadian parliament, that under such circumstances the administration should have the final word taking of course the responsibility of it and having to abide the judgment of parliament. My hon. friend has stated and stated truly that the reports of the Auditor General have been filled year after year with a diversion of opinion between him and the administration, but if that is the case he has it in his power to make any report he wants to make and to make it as strong as he pleases. There is no authority over him, there is no control, he is absolutely independent. He has the power to make the case as strong as possible and to bring it to the attention of parliament which is the court of appeal to decide between him and the government. I do not think that any more salutary check could be placed upon the administration of public moneys in any country.

This check only comes after the harm is done.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Yes, but the harm can be undone by parliament, which can censure the government for haying acted contrary to the opinion of the Auditor General, and that is the only possible solution of the difficulty. If the Auditor General had power to do as he liked, without any control over him. doss the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) deny that the consequences might be to stop the wheels of government. For instance, last year the Auditor General had the opinion at one time, that he could deprive the members of parliament of their indemnity. He -was right or he was wrong ; but members of parliament were not slow to complain that he was wrong, or, that if he were right, then, some means should be found to solve the difficulty. There may be civil servants or contractors to whom the government owes1 money, and there must be some power to decide as to whether they shall be paid or not. It seems to me that the proper authority to decide in such a case is the body which is intrusted by parliament to administer the affairs of the nation. If they go wrong, then they are responsible to parliament and it is for parliament Jo decide upon their conduct. If this is not a sound principle, then all our formalities of government are useless, and we had better have something like they have in Russia and make the Auditor General himself the omnipotent adviser as to when and where payments are to be made. For my part, I think there is in England more political wisdom in matters of government

than in any other country in the world. I do not believe there is a country under the sun where the principles of responsible government are so well understood and; practiced as in England, and I may point out that our Audit Act is copied word for word from the Act in force in England. Although my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) declared that the powers of the Auditor General should be supplemented in some way. I noticed that he was careful not to mention any one particular in which they should be supplemented.

I merely asked for a committee, and I realize that it would come with poor grace from me to lay down rules as to what should be done by that committee. I did throw out some suggestions, very few, but my chief object was to get this committee appointed and leave it to them to decide.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did uot expect that my hon. friend' would lay down any cast iron rules, but we had the right to expect that he would not remain absolutely silent as to the reasons which he would indicate for the consideration of the committee. The hon. gentleman thinks that the Treasury Board has too great power over the Auditor General, and he thinks that once the Auditor General has given an opinion that he ought not pay any appropriation that is asked for by a department, the Auditor General's opinion should not be revised by the Treasury Board. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) has uot told us by what authority the Auditor General's opinion should be revised, nor whether the Auditor General's opinion should be final. For my part I do not think we should appoint a committee, for I do not believe that any better arrangement can be found than the one provided for now in the Audit Act.
Perhaps my hon. friend will pardon me for saying that it is my opinion that everything he has said with regard to the powers of the Auditor General, and with regard to the necessity of this committee, was merely a preface to the discussion of the Davis contract. I shall not pretend to discuss the Davis contract in detail, but I may be permitted1 to give the hon. gentleman my opinion as to its general outlines. The hon. gentleman complains that when we made the contract of 1900, we did not ask for tenders, but the hon. gentleman knows that the second contract of 1900, be it wise or unwise, was simply a completion of and implementing of the contract of 1896. I understand that my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) has no very serious objection to the contract of 1896. He called it a prudent contract, and in many ways I am disposed to agree with him. It provided that Mr. M. P. Davis was to furnish electric light and electric power to work the machinery on the canal.
It provided a price at which that was to be done. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) says that that was a prudent contract, and it being a prudent contract the new government coming into office could not have done better than to have accepted it. The hon. gentleman (Mr, Lennox) cannot seriously complain then that we did not ask for tenders to light the Cornwall canal, when we had a contract already made between Mr. Davis and the government for lighting that canal. In fact we were precluded from calling for tenders. Let us go further, if the contract of 1896 was prudent, was the contract of 1900 imprudent ? It was provided in the contract of 1896 that Mr. Davis was to develop electric power, and having developed it. he was to supply the Cornwall canal with electricity and with motive power for working the machinery of the canal. It was provided that the price should be thirty cents per light per night, and $63 per annum per horse-power.
In 1900, Mr. Davis wanted to implement his contract. He was then in the process of developing the power as therefore ready to supply the lights to the government and to furnish the horse-power for the Cornwall canal. But before he finally put in his apparatus it was indispensable for him to know the quantity of light and the number of horse-power required. My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) will agree with this. Mr. Davis could not put up t'he plant, he could not put up his machinery, he could not take a step to fulfil his contract until he knew exactly the maximum of light and the maximum horse-power that would be needed. He would not have the same plant to supply a maximum of fifty lights as to supply a maximum of 250 lights : he would not instal the same plant for 100 horse-power as he would if he had to furnish 400 horse-power, and therefore it became necessary that the chief engineer of railway department should determine the amount of power and light required and to form a contract accordingly. Thus was made the contract of 1900 which provided that there should be a maximum of 250 lights and a maximum of 400 horse-power to work the machinery of the canal. My hon. friend does not state that these figures are in any way exaggerated. It has been shown beyond doubt in the record that these figures were not exaggerated, but my hon. friend says : You are paying for light which was supplied in winter when there was no necessity for it. The answer is very obvious. When Mr. Davis had put up this plant it did not matter to him in the least whether the canal was lit or not lit, because the moment he had installed his plant upon the Cornwall canal, that plant being moved by machinery, it was of no consequence to him, as has been abundantly 1 proved, whether the lights were used or not:

the eost was the same and all the time the same. Therefore all of the argument made by my hon. friend is beside the point and does not apply in this matter.
Let me call the attention of the committee to the reports of the experts in reference to the examination and it will be seen that it disposes of three-quarters of my hon. friend's argument. The experts say :
In an electric plant where the motive power is water, the cost of operating is practically the same whether the plant carries a -load or not. It follows that the price of electrical energy cannot reasonably be based on energy supplied, but must in whole or in a large part take into consideration the capacity of machinery at the disposal of the service.
Therefore, Sir. it matters not whether the machinery which had been placed there to supply a maximum of 250 lights, which it is admitted is necessary in summer, was operated in winter or not, the expenditure was the same for the contractor, and it had to be paid. Everything was based on the value of the plant installed by the contractor :
The machinery and station capacity placed at the disposal of the government for this service does not depend on the number of arc lamps in actual service, but is entirely fixed by the maximum number called for at any one time.
Although the energy consumed may vary, the generating plant capacity is1 not changed. Moreover the energy available, but not supplied, cannot be sold to any other party, for systems at present employed to do this service keep a constant draught of current independently of the lights in use. The station operating expenses are not changed, the only possible difference would be in the cost of carbons, trimming and care of the lamps, which would not amount to more than $200 to $300 per year.
This disposes I think altogether of all the objections made by my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox).

I do not think so. If my right hon. friend will permit me, the objection I take is this. How is it explained. when the government had committed themselves to a $52,000 expenditure that within a year or two afterwards, they could make a new contract and cut off a matter of $22,000 a year ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I can give the explanation very easily. I was simply justifying the contract of 1000 upon the fact that that expenditure had to be calculated upon the amount of energy necessary to furnish the light and to move the machinery. The Auditor General objected to this and the Treasury Board overruled him, and I think I was right in saying that the Treasury Board was acting within its rights because the Auditor General, even in the opinion of the legal gentleman whom he con-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
suited, Mr. Aylesworth, was altogether wrong legally, and if he was wrong legally, the Treasury Board was right in overruling him. But after the Treasury Board had overruled the Auditor General the matter was taken up again. He had done what was suggested by the report of the Committee on Finance which was quoted a moment ago by my hon. friend. He had gone into the merits of this contract and the objections which he had made, the reasoning which he advanced, and the views which he had set forth were such as made it appear to the government that it was advisable to have the contract investigated by experts, and this is what was found, this is the reason we modified the contract. There is no alteration at all in the number of lights required ; it was stated and was found that the maximum of 250 lights was right. But, Sir, it happened also that the government Department of Railways and Canals have not yet installed all the machinery to move the weirs, locks and bridges and therefore, the amount of energy. 400 horse-power was not required at that time. It will be required later on, in fact 435 horse-power will he required when all the machinery has been installed. We therefore decided that since all the machinery was not installed and since 400 horse-power was not necessary at this moment, hut only 125 horse-power, that we would pay only for 125 horse-power. Let me call my hon. friend's attention to this fact which is very plainly set forth in the new contract :
Upon the present installation being added to or increased, pursuant to such requisitions, payment therefor shall be computed and made as follows :-the present installation, requiring for efficient operation a line load estimated at one hundred and eleven horse-power, is taken, for the purpose of this agreement (with allowances for extra line load, at one hundred and [DOT]twenty-five horse-powers, and shall form the basis of computation. The additional installation, according to capacity, shall be estimated on the same ratio of line load (with the same ratio of allowances for extra line load), -the proportion of the capacity of the present installation to one hundred and twenty-five being always adhered to in the result.
This is the reason why we modified the contract which we had made. My hon. friend stated that there was quite a difference in the cost to the government of the lighting and the supply of energy for the Cornwall and Soulanges canals. My hon. friend is altogether wrong in this. In the Cornwall canal he has taken notice only of the actual salaries, and has taken no notice of the wear and tear nor of the interest on the capital supplied. My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) makes comparison between the present expenditure of the government for lighting and the expenditure for that purpose when the canal was lighted with coal oil. If my hon. friend is ready

to blame the government for having substituted electricity for coal oil, we are prepared to take the blame, but I do not think that those who use the canal will take the same view as he does. For my part I give credit to the late Minister of Railways (Mr. Haggart) for having been the first to introduce the system of lighting our canals by electricity. Not only should we have our canals lit by electricity, but I hope to see the St. Lawrence all the way down lit in this way, and then navigation will be much more safe than it has been.

At this late hour I shall not make any very lengthy remarks. As regards the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox), I had a good deal of experience, when I was Minister of Railways, with the present Auditor General. He has powers equal to those given to any Auditor General in any country I kuow of. Let him have all the possible powers he can desire to draw the attention of the country to any anomaly or wrong there may be in the government accounts, and I have no objection, but the idea of making him the arbiter and sole judge as to the expenditure of the country is another question altogether. Our public expenditure is a matter in which the government must rule. Whether the government administer affairs wisely or badly, the country has given them that power and has not given it to the Auditor General. The proposition of my hon. friend is to give the Auditor General the power of judging whether an expenditure has been properly voted by parliament or not, and to take from the government, after he has expressed his opinion, the power of overruling him. It would be impossible to carry on the government if any such rule were established. Let us by all means have a true and faithful audit ; and where there is any wrong done by the government, let the Auditor General report upon it and draw attention to it in the fullest possible manner, and goodness knows he exercises that power to the fullest extent.
I have said enough upon that point, and I intend to make some remarks, which must necessarily be brief, on the other question raised. I do not wish to adjourn the debate, because we may not have another opportunity of reaching the motion again this session. In the matter of leasing water powers upon the canals, what is the system which has been adopted ever since we have had a government ? It is this. We first get a report from the department as to the value of the horse-power in any particular canal. If the energy or power is at the disposition of the government, we first fix a price per horse-power. Then it is the duty of the minister to see that the horsepower is utilized for the development of the particular section of the country in which the canal is situated. That has been the
rule hitherto followed on all the canals. I have never heard of any horse-power or of any power on any canal being offered to public competition. That was the plan, adopted on the Cornwall canal. It was necessary, on account of the erection of the Shiek's Island dam, that a waste weir should be built for the purpose of letting-the water out of the dam in qase of repairs. At the end of that, there was the possibility of energy being utilized for the purpose of electric lighting or other purposes. What I wish the government to do is this. I would ask it to bring down all the documents in the office of Railways and Canals and to give the names of the parties who have applied for that particular power. I would like to have the dates of the applications, &c., the report of the deputy minister and the minister regarding the value of the power. I want also the report in reference to the leasjng of this particular work and the price that ought to be paid for the lights on the canal. To my own knowledge I ordered the deputy minister to inquire into the prices that were paid in the different cities in Canada, particularly Ottawa and places where there was plenty of waterpower available ; and the prices which he recomended us to pay is the lowest that was known in Canada at that date. I also instructed him to inquire what was the value per horse-power of the energy required for the purpose of working the different gates and the swings of the different bridges. As my right hon. friend has said, I was the first in Canada to decide upon lighting the canals by electricity, generated by water-powers along the canal, and to use the electric power for the purpose of opening and shutting the gates and swinging the bridges. There was not at that time in Canada any electric energy, that I know of, generated by water-power, sold by the horsepower. I asked the deputy minister of Railways to report as to the value, and he based the value upon what power could have been generated by the actual use of a particular work. He arrived at $63 per horse-power, and his report showed that instead of 400" horse-power being required to open and shut the gates, 50 would be all that was necessary. The newspapers are giving importance to the fact that this bargain was made on the eve of an election, that the price was an exorbitant one, that the price now paid in the city of Ottawa is $15 per horse-power. There is a report, it is true, in the Auditor General's Report, which shows that the bargain I made was a fair bargain at the time. No person would erect a plant, such as was proposed, down there for the purpose of generating power, if it was only 50 horse-power which was required. The price agreed on was $63, which the experts in my department recommended as a fair price." The price paid for lighting the canal was the lowest paid for arc lighting in any

part of Canada. The water used for this particular work was taken from the summit level of the canal and might have interfered with those who had powers below; and I made the condition that if it interfered with navigation or -works operated below or any works to be hereafter erected, the government would have the right of stoppage.
The only right given to the agent was this -the right to deepen Hoople's creek to take into the level of the Cornwall canal sufficient water for the undertaking that he proposed and the development of this energy for electrical purposes. He had a perfect right to that. The only question is were the government receiving a fair price as compensation for the privileges they gave him? I say they were receiving a fair price, larger price per horse-power than was given for any undertaking on the Lachine, Welland or Cornwall canals. There were no exceptional advantages given to Mr. Davis. I do not think that Mr. Davis was an applicant in the first place, but that he acquired the right from some other person ; or, at least, that some other person joined with him in making application. I do not remember the circumstances, but I know that the contract had nothing to do with an election. What I want to get from the department is when the application was entertained. It strikes me that it was in 1894 and was entertained in 1895 and that the Order in Council was passed on the 17th of February, 1896. I would like the memorandum to Council, which, I think, was 7th February, 1896. The Order in Council a few days before election did not alter the order of 17th February one bit, except that the description of the land in the memorandum, if I remember aright, was larger in extent than in the Order in Council of June 23rd or June 22nd or whatever the date was. The only change was to restrict the area of land to be granted to carry on the undertaking. So that the lease was founded, not on an order passed a few days before an election, but on an order passed on the 17th of February and a memorandum of 7th February, and a bargain made months-yes, I venture to say a year-before. Yet the Auditor General draws the attention of the people to the extraordinary coincidence that this was done on the eve of an election.
Who says that ?

The Auditor General. He speaks of it as a remarkable coincidence that the Order in Council was passed a few days before an election and the lease a couple of days afterwards, and also that the changes made by hon. gentlemen opposite were during an election. The facts are as I have given them; and an election had nothing to do with the matter. The result of an election may have done something to hasten the signing of the lease. After an election, the head of the department may change. In view of that, what is done ? The minister Mr. HAGGART.
sees to it that every bit of the work in the department is cleared up, if it can be cleared up. If he has made promises for senator-ships he tries to get the Order in Council through which is to carry the amount. In this case the Order in Council has been passed that there was nothing to do but sign the lease. It was simply an item in the back-work of the department, and was carried out by the minister and was brought over to the council to receive consent. And this is the scandal that some of the newspapers say is greater than the Pacific scandal-a greater scandal than has exercised the people for a number of years past. I do not know what hon. gentlemen oxiposite have done ; I am only defending what took place in my own time. It was a simple transaction and perfectly justifiable. As to the figures, I could not follow my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox's) figures very well, but they seemed a little confused in reference to the Soulanges canal.
I am sure that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) will find the figures perfectly correct. He can go over them any time he likes.
I think I can show they are not correct.
Then do so.

The cost of the installation on the Soulanges canal is given on the authority of Mr. Hoffmeister, resident engineer of the Canadian General Electric Company on the Soulanges canal, at $197.000 ; then for lighting the canal and operating all the lock gates, sluice gates and highway bridges by electrical energy, $160,000. The electrical energy which Mr. Davis supplies according to Mr. McDougall's statements amounts to $15,800 a year. But if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) will look at the preceding part of it he will find the cost of operating it by this gentleman's estimate is $10,000 a year. The cost of the plant was, approximately $225,000 with contingencies and items that might be under-estimated, making an addition of $33,750 was $258,750.
That is the Cornwall canal.
Yes. And the cost of operating, if ail the plant ran continuously would exceed $10,000 a year.
I did not mention that at all.	.
Then what would be the value of that ? Say 12 per cent for depreciation and interest-that would be nearly $30,000 alone and after that $10,000 for operating, and you have $40,000 a year.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) seems to think Mr. Davis is losing by it.

He is not making much, if the cost is as this gentleman states.

According to the report from Mr. Keefer, the engineer employed by the Auditor General to report upon the value of the property, the cost is $225,000, with addition for contingencies and items under-estimated $33,750 or a total of $258,750.
The Soulanges canal, which is the only one I mentioned, cost $190,000.
Call it $200,000 and allow 12 per cent-
We count it at 8 per cent.

But surely you allow for depreciation in the value of the plant of eight or ten per cent. The cost, according to the hon. gentleman, is $200,000 ; 10 per cent on that is $20,000 as the cost of operating the plant, which is $5,000 less than the Auditor General makes it. I do not wish to go into the details, as I suppose all the papers will be contained in the report when it is brought down. I want, first of all, the memorandum from myself, or whoever was minister at the time. I do not know whether 1 made a memorandum or not, I mean the memorandum to Council of the 7th of February, on which the Order in Council was passed. Then I want the Order in Council of the 23rd of June, and all applications in the department in reference to this particular work, and particularly the report of the deputy head of the department as to the value of the lighting and horse-power, and as to the value which I ought to attach to the water power which was leased to Mr. Davis.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will follow the example of those who preceded me, and be brief, taking up the facts in their chronological order. On the Sth of February, 1896, the then Minister of Railways and Canals made a memorandum to Council recommending that authority be given to lease to Mr. M. P. Davis a certain amount of land in the immediate vicinity of the Cornwall canal- the description of the land is in the memorandum here-and, in addition, a ter-tain quality of water power. That memorandum, dated on the Sth of February, 1896. was adopted by Council on the 18th of February, 1896, on which day an Order in Council passed authorizing the leasing of this land and of this water power. On the 2oth of June, 1896, a lease was passed which was merely for the purpose of giving effect to that which had been decided on the 18tli of February, 1896. Now, what is the lease ? The lease is to be found on page 6 of the Auditor General's Report, and refers to a lot of land at the lower end of Sheik's island. I will not read that. That which is important is contained in the next paragraph, and that paragraph is of such importance that I will read a certain portion of it :
And as pursuant to the said lot of land, and subject to the restrictions, reservations and
conditions contained, described and expressed herein and in the annexed general terms and conditions, the lessor has granted, demised and leased, and by these presents does grant, demise and lease to the lessee, the use for manufacturing and mechanical purposes, as hereinafter set forth,

I would like to draw the attention of the House to what I am now going to say, because I want the House to understand what was given to Mr. Davis. What was given to him was the use of-
-so much of the surplus water, if any, on lot number 30 level, Cornwall canal, as the lessor may deem advisable, after navigation and existing mills and mill sites hereinafter to he leased, are supplied

He is to get the surplus water, whatever it may be, that is left after all the necessities of navigation are complied with, after all the mills then in existence have been satisfied, and after all the mills to be built hereafter on all the mill sites are satisfied with water-he gets what is left. That is the contract, that is the lease.
-and the lessee shall also have the privilege of using, at a weir hereafter to be constructed by him, on or adjacent to the land hereby demised and as shown on the plan hereunto annexed, for the purpose of power, the amount of water flowing and to flow into the said canal from Hoople's creek, and any increased flow of water into the said canal from the said creek through any works hereafter to be constructed by the lessee.
The next clause provides for the term of the lease. The clause which has reference to that reads as follows :
The privileges, rights and easements are granted for a term of tw'enty-one years from and after the 1st day of July, 1896, and ended on the 1st day of July, 1917, and thereafter for a term or period of twenty-one years, renewable as is provided and mentioned in the annexed general terms and conditions.
Now, an attempt has been made designedly to lead the public astray with reference to the condtions of this lease. It has been falsely stated to the public that the original lease had in contemplation a lease for twenty-one years. As a matter of fact, the original lease had in contemplation, not only by the terms I mentioned last, but also by the terms governing all leases to which reference is made in this, an extension of that lease to 1980, or for eighty-four years. That is the term of the original lease. Then, in addition, you have got the power leased, you have got the object of the lease, you have got the term of the lease-eighty-four years -and you have got all that is necessary to constitute a lease of the power to Mr. Diavis. But in connection with that lease there is a reservation, that is to say, the government provide that while they give that power to Mr. Davis on the terms I have indicated, for a rental of $1,000 a year, for the period I have mentioned, he is then obliged to sup-

ply them with power for the purposes of the canal, to move the locks, gates, sluices, and so forth, and also for the erection of a lighting power for the canal. That is the reservation of the lease. The lease provides also :
That the lessee shall supply electric power to the satisfaction of the chief engineer of Railways and Canals for the working of all the locks on the Cornwall canal at $63 per horse-power per annum.
That is the price fixed in the original document. Then it goes on to say that in addi tion to that he shall supply and work electric arc lights of not less than 2,000 candle power, in perfect working order, at such points and in such number as shall, from time to time, be deemed necessary by the chief engineer. So he is obliged to supply power, he is obliged to supply light to an extent that may be ordered by the chief engineer. Then you have got this extraordinary provision in this document to the effect that, not only in the case of failure on his part to perform any of the conditions of the lease the whole thing is forfeited to the Crown, but also that at any time after he has made his expenditures the government may turn around and, after giving Mr. Davis a year's notice, take over the whole lousiness from him-his plant, machinery, everything, paying him for it the then value with 5 per cent added. They have at any time the right to enter into possession of the whole thing, take it all out of his hands. That is the original contract. My hon. friend spoke of that contract as having met yvith the disapprobation of the Auditor Gen-"eral.
That is quite true. The Auditor General, dealing with this matter, found it necessary to criticise everything. He starts out with criticising the original contract and suggests all sorts of sinister motives in connection with the making of it. On the 29th of May, 1902, the Auditor General, at page 19 of his report, says that this contract is defective because it does not make proper provision for the payment of the price foi; the light. Then he goes on to say that the letting of this contract is a violation of the Act, 49 Vic., chap. 37, which provides for inviting public tenders in letting contracts of this sort. I do not require to deal with that part of the question because my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has dealt with it. I venture to say, however, that there have been hundreds and hundreds if not thousands of contracts for leases of water powers made in this country, there was one made within the last few days, and it has never been suggested that these leases of water powers should come under the public works Act.
Does the hon. gentleman understand me to advance the idea that leases should not be made without tender V

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I never would have accused my hon. friend of having harboured such a thought. I am dealing with the position of the Auditor General. Then, at page 20 of the Auditor General's Report, I find a letter dated the 4th June. 1902, in which he deals again with the original contract. He says :
Apart from the very manifest principle which should hold in such cases, that the country should be protected from applicants getting prices at their own dictation, there are two Acts, viz. : The Audit Act, section 33, and the Act with reference to the Department of Railways, section 11, which seem to have been disregarded.
Then at page 25 he deals with the same contract. He says :
Then I may call your attention to the rather singular fact that there were two arrangements in connection with the matter : the first was made 11 days before the election of June 23, 1896.	.
Of course, he is out there because the contract bears date the 25th of June, two days after. But he is so anxious to find fault that he says the contract was made on the 23rd of June, 1896, and of course he suggests all sorts of improper motives on the part of those who made the contract. The Auditor General deals with it again at page 26 of his report. He says :
It must be forgotten that in addition to the $51,000 a year, Mr. Davis also has the right to all rental which the water power will bring.
Then again at page 29 he discusses it in these words :
The government in 1896 might, it seems to me, have'kept in view the fact that the first-class water power which was being leased to Mr. Davis should have been held by the government until a lessee was found who would have accorded the government power and light on the most favourable terms,
Now I am done with that part of his criticism. But, what do we find at page 35 7 Hon. gentlemen who have followed me in whit I have said will recollect that portion of his criticism in which he states that this contract was made on the eve of an election. What does he say at page 35 of his report '! Under date of October 11, 1902, he says :
Bear in mind that the present Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals was in office when the agreement of 1896 was made, that he presumably was either the author of the carefully prepared agreement of 1896, the one which so fully guards all the public interests by providing against a successful claim by the contractor, for either electric light or energy, the use of which is not obtained by the public.
There you have the Auditor General's views as expressed in his own report in reference to this contract at these different dates. But that is not all. Let us take the opinions of the experts who were selected with the approval of the Auditor General to

deal with this matter. You have Mr. Herdt, who is a professor at McGill College, Montreal, and who from a technical standpoint is one of the most competent electrical engineers in the country. You have also Mr.l Dion Who is at the top of his profession and Mr. Parke, of Toronto. I find, at page 45 of the report, that they say :
We are of the opinion that-for the time (1896) and the service to he rendered, namely, to supply power for 24 hours per day in small units, and to furnish lamps and light them, the whole scattered over a course covering many miles-the prices to be paid were reasonable. It has been possible since, under certain conditions, mode of delivery, &c., and in very large quantities, to sell power ajt comparatively low rates, but the lease must be judged from the conditions prevailing at the time it was made and what might reasonably be expected as to the future from the data at hand.
That Is as to the price. Then they go on to deal with the time which the lease had to run and they say :
Under the lease the lessee was required to construct costly works, and it was necessary to have it cover a long period of time.
So, yon have the justification in so far as these gentlemen are concerned for the price paid and for the period during which the lease was to run. Now that is the contract of which the Auditor General speaks ill such high terms of praise at page 35 of his report and which is approved of by the engineers whose names I gave a moment ago. 1 say now, that, dealing with the contract made in 1896, and of which the Auditor General speaks in such high terms, that not a single line of that contract, not a single word of that contract has been changed by the present government. It remains in the condition in which it was and there has been no departure from it to the slightest extent. It has been suggested that the renewal of that contract for 21 years is provided for by the contract of 1900. Nothing of the sort. It was provided for by the original contract, wisely and properly provided i'or, because there is a clause in the original contract which enables the government at any time to step in and take possession ot the whole work paying the contractor merely the then value of the work which they take over. What was done by the second contract of 1900 ? By the second contract ot 1900, provision was made merely for the number of lights to be used on the canal and for the amount of horse-power which was required in connection with the working ot the gates, locks, weirs and so on. As I said a moment ago this was provided for in the original contract of 1896, which also provided that the engineer of the government, should, when the necessity arose, that is when the canal was ready to be put into operation, determine the number of lights and also determine the amount of horse-power required to effectually operate
the canal. The engineer did that ; that is to say that when the canal was finished in 1900 it became necessary to light it. The engineer was applied to and he said it would be necessary to have 250 lights to properly light the canal. Is it doubted for a moment that that was the proper number of lights '! Experience establishes the fact now, after the canal has been in operation, that we have not one light more than is necessary and as we have had a comparison made with the Soulanges canal I will take occasion to show that notwithstanding the statement made by the Auditor General and by the hon. member for Simcoe there are fewer lights in operation on the Cornwall canal than on the Soulanges canal. You will find that the experts say that the number of lights required by the engineer is merely sufficient for the purpose of lighting the canal and in addition to that we have our practical experience of the operation of the canal and when the engineer said that 250 lights were absolutely necessary our experience has shown that he was absolutely correct. What was done in 1900 ? I shall not ask the House to take my view of it. 1 do not want the House to take my opinion because I was not a member of the government at that time and had nothing to do with the making of this contract, although I think it was a very ^proper contract notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman for Simcoe has said. I will lake the opinion of the gentleman selected by the Auditor General to advise him in respect to this matter. I take the opinion of the gentleman selected by the Auditor General to advise him in respect to this matter ; and in regard to the contract of 1900, Mr. Aylesworth says :
There appears an Order in Council of October 9th, 1900, authorizing the agreement of October 19th, 1900, under which the claim to payment is now made, but it is to be observed that this agreement of October, 19, 1900, in fact amounts to nothing more than a fixing of the quantities of electric horse-power and electric light the contractor is to supply.
The original contract was not departed from to the extent of a hair's breadth ; all that was done by the supplemental contract of 1900, was to do that which the orignal contract had in contemplation, viz. : to provide for the number of lights required, and the horse power necessary, and which were fixed by the engineer who made the original contract. As Mr. Aylesworth says, all that was done under the second contract was to fix the number of lights and the quantity of horse-power the contractors were to supply.
The lease previously entered into and dated June 25th, 1896, seems to have conferred upon Mr. Davis the right to supply such electric power and light on the canal as the chief engineer of the department might require, and if it was, under this lease, the right of Mr. Davis to supply the light and power in question, there was no possibility in October, 1900, that

there should be competition, or the consideration of tenders, before the agreement then made with Mr. Davis was entered into.
There is the opinion of the gentleman selected by the Auditor General to advise him on this matter, and who says that in view of the contract made in 1896, Mr. Davis had a fair right under the contract to supply the light and power and that the government had no right to call for tenders and no possibility to provide that there should be competition. I draw the attention of my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) to page 13 of the Auditor General's Report, where he Will find that so far back as the 1st of December, 1901, there were then in operation on the Cornwall Canal, 216 lights. In the report of the experts (page 47) the hon, gentleman will find the following statement :
The agreement of 1900 calls for a minimum of 250 lights and 400 horse-power. The 250 lights appear to be no more than sufficient to light the canal, as the lamps which are placed is 400 feet apart, are not too close for proper illumination.
The experts conSrm the opinion of the e' g nrer of the Department of Railways and Canals, who was himself selected when the contract was made in 1896 to determine the number of lights. There is no doubt about the number of lights, required. And now as to the horse-power required, it was intended that we should have power required to move the locks, and the gates, and the bridges, and to operate the workshops, and in addition to haul boats moving through the canal by means of wenches, run by electric power. This was a new departure inaugurated by my hon. friend (Mr. Hag-gart). When the time came to determine what was required under this contract the government's engineer gave a detailed statement to the effect that to do the work in contemplation it would require 417 horsepower. The contract was made accordingly, and as the Prime Minister pointed out, it would have been lacking in prudence on the part of the contractors to have installed a plapt there without knowing how much power he would require to generate. His contract was to supply not less than 250 lights, and not less than 400 horse-power, and it was proper on his part that he should say : If I am obliged to supply that, give me some assurance that when I have expended my money to supply it, I should have a demand for it. The contractor set to work, and he had his plant installed before the machinery built by the government was ready to use the power. The contractor was ready to supply the electric energy, but the government were not ready to utilize it because it was necessary for the government to determine the extent to which the power should be applied to each particular machine. The contractor said:	I
am ready to supply the power, and you are Mr. FITZPATRICK.	.
not ready to utilize it, and why should I be deprived of the money to which I am entitled under the contract? The government said : Here is a contract which we must abide by, but we have a provision in the contract which enables us to expropriate your plant, and let us see if we can came to a fair understanding about it; we are not ready to utilize the power, but it is not fair to ask us to pay for something we are not getting. It was not the Auditor General who did that, it was the government that did it. Then the government said to the contractor : We have so much plant installed now and for that plant it is necessary for us to have so much horse-power; we will pay you for the power necessary to operate the plant we have installed, and as further plant is installed we will pay you proportionately for the power required for it. There is no mystery about that. We want to keep nothing back in connection with this matter. The whole difficulty arises from the fact that when the government contractor was ready to deliver power the government was not ready to receive it to the extent he was ready to deliver it. In law he was entitled to' be paid because he was ready to execute his part of the contract, but to the credit of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) let it be said there was a provision in that contract by which we could turn around to the contractor and say : Very well ; if you exact your pound of flesh we will exact ours.
You will be entitled to be paid for what you contracted to deliver and what we are prepared to take, but we will expropriate your plant. Mr. Davis, I say it now, never asked for anything to which he was not fairly entitled, and when the matter was properly put to him, all he ever took payment for was what was delivered to the government, notwithstanding, that according to the strict letter of his contract, he might have been paid for more. There is the whole case. What is there in it which we need to hide, and what is there in it to make all this scandal about ? I have not said a word that I have not corroborated by reference to the Auditor General's Report, and not a word that cannot be so corroborated. I do not find any fault with the very deliberate statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox). I want to deal with the Auditor General, who makes a comparison between the cost of the Cornwall and Soulanges canals. In one instance he says : You have the government plant on the Soulanges canal, and the installation there cost so much and the operation costs so much ; and then he says, you have let a contract for the Cornwall canal, and the operation will cost just so much. Let us see if it is possible to compare them. At page 27 of his report the Auditor General says that the cost of installation of the Soulanges canal is $160,000. That statement is contained in his letter, dated July 14th,

1902. He says that -the cost of operation is $5,000 a year ; that is the cost of running a plant, and he puts in $4,800 for interest. He, therefore, says our charges are $9,800. At the time he made that statement, on July 14, he had in' his possession a letter from the man who installed the plant, Mr. Holfmeister, which was written on July 12th, and which will be found on page 29 following of his report. In that letter Mr. Hoffmeister tells him that the total cost of the installation was $200,000. That is on the next page from the page I quoted. At the foot of that page, he tells him that the operating expenses may go up to $5,700. There is the position of the Auditor General with respect to that statement. Then he goes on and says he has derived the cost of installation from his report, and gives it at $100,000. I have a statement from the Chief Engineer of the Department of Railways ; and also one which I have made up from the Auditor General's Report. From the Auditor General's Report it will appear that the cost of installation of the plant was, not $100,000, but $212,820 ; and from the Chief Engineer of the Railway Department, I have a statement carried down to date, which shows that the cost of installation on the Soulanges canal is $218,175, and the cost of operation is not $5,000, as was stated in the letter, the cost of operation is $11,131. If to that cost of operation you add six per cent, which is a very small amount for depreciation of plant, and you add three per cent for interest, you have got $29,000 for the Soulanges canal. His statement here is simply as to' the cost of operation, to which may be added interest-and the government cannot to-day borrow money at 3 per cent -and you cannot allow less than 6 per cent for depreciation. Thus you have $18,000 and if you add to that $11,000 for operation, you have $29,000 as the cost of the Soulanges canal instead of $10,000, practically three times the amount given in the Auditor General's Report.
A statement appears at page 23 of the Auditor General's Report of the amount of power required to operate the Cornwall canal. As a matter of fact, you have two canals at Cornwall, but the Auditor General does not think it necessary to refer to that. There is, however, the old canal and the new canal, both of which have to be equipped and looked after. The new canal has twenty-six locks and two guard-gates. The old canal has twenty lock gates. On the Soulanges, with which he compares this, you have four lift locks, one guard-gate and one guard-lock, as against forty-six on the other. On the new canal you have sluice gates or valves, 26 ; on the old canal, sluice gates or valves, 20. You have six winches on the new canal, five winches on the old canal, and in addition to that you have on the Cornwall canal a workshop which is now being built to provide
for the service on both the Cornwall and Williamsburg canals, and that workshop requires 60 horse-power.
What have you got at the iSoulanges ? Four lift-locks, one guard gate, one guard lock, twenty sluice gates, five weirs and seven bridges. Of these the lock gates, sluice gates and five bridges are worked by electricity. You have no winches and no workshops, although one is being built but is not in operation. How could you, in justice or in conscience, compare the conditions existing at Cornwall with the conditions existing at Soulanges ? There is no comparison to be made between the two. Mr. Schreiber, at page 33, very properly says :
In dealing with the question of the application of electricity to the several purposes of the Cornwall canal operation (which at the present date is a matter of theory and estimate, rather than of conclusive calculation, based on definite experience), provision had to be made, on both the old and new canals, for the lock and guard gates, for the sluice gates or valves, for bridges, and for winches to assist vessels through the locks. In addition, power had to to be furnished for the workshops, which serve not only the Cornwall canal, but also the three canals constituting what is known as the Williamsburg canals.
That is wh'at the Chief Engineer of the Railways and Canals Department says with respect to the Cornwall canal.
What do you state is a fair annual cost of operating the Soulanges canal ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think I can give the average cost of that, because, in my judgment, it altogether depends On what we have to pay to operate that. The price for the power was fixed in 1896. There is no doubt but that at that time the price was fair and reasonable. The amount we will have to pay for the operation of the Cornwall canal is dependent on the amount of power to be used in connection with its operation ; if 200 horse-power is used, 200 times 63 will be the cost; if 400 horse-power is used, then 63 times .400 will be the cost. For 200 horse-power it would be 200 times 63, and for 400 borse-power 400 times 63.
That is operated by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Cornwall is operated by Mr. Davis.
I am asking about Soulanges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot tell any more than my hon. friend. All I know is that up to the present.we have expended $218,175, and that the annual charge, independent of interest and depreciation, was $11,131, and they have not equipped one-half the canal. There are five weirs not equipped, which have no electric plant.
As I understand the hon. minister, he cannot tell us, by way of comparison, how much it does cost on the Sou-langes canal for the same service as Mr. Davis is supplying.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not like to make comparisons. I prefer to state the facts and let my hon. friend make the comparison. My figures are official.
If you will give them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have given them. Perhaps I had better give them again. On the Soulanges canal there are five weirs not equipped. There are two bridges which have not got the necessary appliance to utilize the power. There are no winches to help the vessels through the locks, and you cannot tell what the work is going to cost. But the small equipment that is on it we do know has cost $218,175 and the annual outlay, independent of interest and depreciation is $11,131. But we have something better than that.
When the work is completed, will the work have to be increased on the Soulanges canal ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not an electrical engineer, but I should say it will and 1 will give my reasons. On page 30 of the Auditor General's Report, Mr. Hoffmeister
says :
