The maximum power required for operating the Soulanges canal, that is, if a lockage is made at every lock and all the highway bridges are operated all at the same time, it would only require 40 horse-power.
That is what he tells us. It is only going to take forty horse-power to work the whole canal. Then he goes on to say :
But the average power required with a fairly good traffic passing through the canal, it would only require about 20 to 25 horsepower to operate the canal.
All that is wanted is forty horse-power. What we have got already has cost $218,000 and it will cost $11,000 per year to keep it going, independent of depreciation and interest. Providence protect us from government ownership if that is a sample of it. I do not know that it is necessary forme to go further into this matter. The position I take is this, that the first contract of 1890 was made at a time when it was necessary to dispose of this power, and at that time the term of the lease was fixed, the price of the light to be supplied was fixed, and also of the horse-power.
We wjere not bound to take anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On that point I happen to differ from my hon. friend. All that was left over for this government to do was, when it became necessary to utilize Mr. FITZPATRICK.
the lights and the power, to fix the number of lights and the number of horse-power. That is what was done in 1900. The only difficulty that has arisen arose out of the fact that the contractor was ready to deliver his power before the government was ready to utilize it, and on a strict reading of the contract he was entitled to be paid for the power he was ready to supply. But after having considered the matter, and when it was found that the quantity required would be 126 horse-power, he agreed to reduce his claim to that amount, and in any addition to that up to 400 horse-power, he would be paid at the price fixed in the lease. The contract of 1896 was made by our hon. friends opposite and we think-in the words of the Auditor General-that it was a provident and a wise contract, and we think that the contract we have made is equally provident and wise because it gives effect to that of hon. gentlemen opposite.

I am not going to discuss the question of the Davis contract at all further than to say that in the speech just delivered by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) he has shown an impatience which is hardly the proper accompaniment of a good case. He has taken particular pains to discredit if possible one of the chief officers of this House. The hon. minister is not wanting in courage, but if evidence were wanting I do not think he has given any evidence of it in taking the stand he has done. I am not prepared to say that the Auditor General makes no mistakes or tha't the government made no mistakes, but the House must be very much struck by the admission of the Minister of Justice that a wise provision was put in the contract by the Minister of Railways in the late administration (Mr. Haggart), which they took advantage of when they said to Mr. Davis : We will either use the power of expropriation or you must come down. , Without going into the merits of the contract, I say that the government should have been prepared to utilize all the power that Mr. Davis was ready to furnish them. I cannot agree with what has been said to-night, even by the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), to the effect that the Auditor General should be reduced to the position of a mere clerk in the office.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No one has said that.

That is absolutely the contention of the government and that was the position taken by the Minister of Finance last year. Naturally an officer or that kind will be sometimes wrong. And that the government have greater inducements to do wrong is a thing that must go unchallenged. What is the position of the
/

government-and I refer to no particular government ? It is simply governed by tile political and party exigencies of the case. They have no other guide. They give the people no reason, and the opposition is powerless. The Auditor General makes his protest year after year, but how does that cure it ? The government are not checked by their own supporters. Would the Prime Minister be prepared to say that the government would look for the condemnation of their own party to uphold the Auditor General or check the overruling of his decisions by the government. He knows there is nothing of that kind. As to the case of England, no complaint has ever been made there that the Auditor General encroaches upon the rights of the government. The strong opinion is that the authority of this important office, the Auditor General ought to be increased. But the tendency here is to diminish it. It can hardly he that in every case of difference between the government and the Auditor General the government is invariably and [DOT] wholly right. The Prime Minister himself would not say that.
How about the opposition, are they ever wrong ?

It is not a matter of the opposition. It is a matter with the people. The Auditor General stands between the government and the people. It is not a matter for the opposition at all. If the Auditor General is only to be an officer to see that the columns of figures are added up right and that receipts are duly filed, he will fulfil the duties cut out for him by the Minister of Finance. But should not the Auditor General have more power than that ? Should not he call in question irregularities? Should not he consider whether the expenditures are made according to law ? I think nobody will contend that there should not be an officer charged with that duty. We find the two extremes, on one side the contention that the Auditor General is never wrong and the other that the ministry is always right. True, the Prime Minister said, and I think it was repeated by another hon. gentleman opposite, that the remedy is for the Auditor General to make his report, which comes before parliament and can be here discussed, and parliament is to be the judge. But, is parliament an unbiassed body ? Under our system of party government-using the words in the restricted sense .in which we generally use them-can it be said that parliament is a body without bias to judge such matters ? The ministry will be supported, and not a man on the other side will venture to call its actions in question.
What remedy would the hon. member propose ?
I do not think I would be justified in presuming to offer a specific remedy.
How about a genera' remedy ?
I do not know what my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) means ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) said he could not offer a specific remedy. I suggest that a general remedy would be sufficient.
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) would be more general in his silence, it would be better. He is merely trying to be clever.
Not with you, not for a moment.

I have escaped the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) because I have rarely found it my duty to reply to what he has to say. That is the only way to escape the honourable member's filth, f said a moment ago that I was not prepared to offer a specific remedy, but what I do offer the suggestion that this is of sufficient importance-and I think the Prime Minister might agree to that-to justify an investigation. There is no proposal to change in any sense the authority of the government. I am not contending that the Auditor General is all right. But surely there should be some medium between the two extremes, and, the way to find this medium is worthy of inquiry. I do not think the country will receive with great favour the remarks made on behalf of the government.
If I have exceeded the time I should have taken at this hour, I apologize to the House. I think the matter is worthy of greater consideration than has been given to it.

My only apology for saying anything at this hour in the morning is that the works referred to in this discussion are located in the county I represent. The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) in his very able argument in favour of the motion he has presented to the House, took occasion to bring up the question of the lighting of the Cornwall canal. Now, I do not pretend to go over the ground that has been gone over so well this evening, but I will endeavour to confine myself to a very few points. The hon. member for Simcoe laid some stress upon the statement contained in one of the letters of the Auditor General calling attention to the fact that power could be purchased by Mr. Eddy at $15 per horse-power, while, in this contract, the price was fixed at $63 per horse-power. That price per horse-power, as has been explained by the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, was fixed by the Order in Council and in the lease which was executed in June, 1890. I have here a copy of the Order in Council of February 18, 1896, under which this property was to be leased

to Mr. Davis and under which he agreed to supply electric power for the working of the locks on the Cornwall canal at $03 per horse-power, and also direct current arc lights of not less than 2,000 candle power at 30 cents per light per night. Now, it struck me, when I first read the correspondence in connection with this matter that the price charged for power was an excessive price.
I do not think I would detain the House in discussing this matter if it were not that it seems to me the press have got an entirely erronous idea of it. and I think it is well that the facts should be thoroughly ventilated. After hearing the explanation of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) I can readily understand why the price was fixed at $6 per horse-power. I can understand that no contractor would develop power, the fifty horse-power which was supposed to be at that time the amount required for the canal, at a rate of $15 per horse power. It is possible in large deals to supply power for such a concern as Eddy's, in blocks of three, or four, or five hundred horse-power. But that is an entirely different proposition to supplying power in small units. Now we find on the Cornwall canal-I think I am familiar with almost every foot of it-that not only for the new canal, as the Minister of Justice explained, but also for the old canal, we have the different wreirs and we have the bridges. Now this ' power has got to be suplied in units running down as low as one and a half or two horse-power. That means that there have to be transformers to take away down to these small units. The consequence is that there is a bank of transformers at every lock gate for the whole distance of eleven and a half miles, and there are transformers at the sluiceways and at the bridges. So I say the power delivered in these small units is of much greater value than the power delivered in large quantities of 100 or 150 horse-power at a time. However, the fact remains that by the Order in Council signed by Sir Mackenzie Bowell. in February. 1896.- the price was fixed, and there could he no variation in regard to that.
I wish to say this, that I think, irrespective of politics, the residents of Stormont desire to see our canal lighted by electricity. We desire to see our canal operated by electrical energy ; we desire to see this power developed so that if there is any surplus energy after supplying the requirements of the canal, it may be utilized for manufacturing purposes in that district. I am not going to compare the cost of coal oil with electricity. Where it is possible to aid navigation with electric lights, I think it is the duty of a progressive government to give the advantage of electric lights and also the advantage of electric power. Let me go back a little further. The Conservative government that *was in power some years ago built at Sheik's Mr. PRINGLE.
Island a dam from which this power is derived, and that Sheik's Island dam I think I am correct in saying has been an immense aid to navigation on the St. Lawrence river. Instead of vessels taking five or six hours to pass through the Cornwall canal, by that Shiek's Island dam to-day they pass through in half the time. Now by having all our locks operated by electricity, and the canal lighted by electricity, boats can pass through at- any hour of the night, and on any kind of night, with perfect safety, and they also go through the locks very much more readily.
If these articles that I have read in the newspapers were any way true, I would feel it was my duty in this House to criticise the contract that has been made. But, Sir. I have looked into this matter as carefully as I could, and I can see nothing unreasonable in this contract. I can see no unreasonable revenue going to the contractor. Why Sir, take the contract as it stands today. We find that the greatest revenue which he can receive, to the limit of a cent, is $29,850. We find by the evidence of experts that the cost of operating, maintenance, &c., would be $20,000, made up in this way :	They allow $9,400 for depreciation,
then they allow for operating expenses $5,800. Let me say here that I have knowledge that the operating expenses at $5,800 are nearly $2,000 too small. The pay-list of the contractor to-day for operation is $700 a month, which would be $8,400 a year, though I am willing to take these figures for the purpose of argument. Then they allow for accidents not elsewhere provided for, $1,000', rental of water power, $1,000, making in all $20,000. Deduct that $20,000 from the utmost revenue that he can receive at the present time, $29,850, and you have net $9,850, or less than 4 per cent upon his investment on that plant. Some one may say : What is that investment'.' I am informed the investment is over $250,000, but I am willing to take the statement of the Auditor General's engineer, the engineer that he put on of his own volition, Mr. Keefer. Mr. Keefer estimates the cost of that plant at $258,000. Mr. Hoffmeister and Mr. Munro also went into that matter. Mr. Hoffmeister put it at $204,000. But I understand the actual investment on that plant is $250,000. So the contractor at the present time has les than 4 per cent upon his investment of $250,000.	.
Let me say another thing in regard to this canal. Last year an accident occurred by lighting which cost the contractors $5,000. That is not provided for in any way, that is a contingency he has got to meet. The winter before last during the ice shove, a large number of bis poles and his electrical appliances were destroyed. I happened myself that afternoon to be watching that ice shove, and saw' these poles snapped off like pipe stems. He suffered much loss then

Only a short time ago there was an accident on the line. A poor unfortunate man through some carelessness of his own came in contact with a live wire and was killed. His widow could not have brought a successful action, but he gave a generous settlement to the family of the man who was killed. Now all these accidents in connection with a plant of that sort have got to be taken into consideration. Why, Sir, we have heard here about the Soulanges canal, and about the expense of operating it. I took the trouble myself to go into the Auditor General's Report to. see whether the statement made by the Auditor General was correct, and I found, just as the Minister of Justice has stated to-night, that the cost of these works was very much larger than the Auditor General puts it. He makes a ridiculous statement in regard to the costs of operation. The cost of operation is away in excess of the figures that have been given by the Auditor General. I found further that they are also liable to just the same accidents we have on the Cornwall canal. It might be well to refer you to the page of the report to show you where it costs them some thousands of dollars for little accidents that occur and are likely to occur at any time on those works, and that is a risk that the contractor, or the owners of the work, have got to incur. Let us take one little accident that occurred on March 10th 1901.
Repairs on pole lines due to storm Sunday night March 10, 1901, $2,452.49.
I only give that as an instance of the accidents that are likely to occur.

I understand that in your calculation you had allowed a certain amount for depreciation which you said, with interest on the investment on this contract, did not exceed 4 per cent. Have you in these figures taken into consideration those contingencies and accidents on the lines and that sort of thing ?

No, I have not taken these contingencies into consideration. I was speaking of the additional expenses incurred on the Soulanges canal. These are expenses which are incident to these works. I do not think I will trespass upon the time of the House any further. The ground has been covered so completely by those who have spoken before me. I was rather struck myself, at the decision arrived at by the Treasury Board and afterwards to find that they rescinded that order. I could not quite understand it, but we have now had the explanation of the hon. the Minister of Justice. I felt that the decision of the Treasury Board was a right decision. Of course I view it from the legal standpoint. Mr. Aylesworth, at page 39 of the report gives his opinion in very clear language He says :
I think that was the position of matters and the right of the government in the premises
138.	.
prior to the agreement of October 19, 1900, but by the document of the last mentioned date the number of such lights has been, I think, fixed by the agreement of the parties at not less than 250, and I think, therefore, that if on any night any lights at all are required Mr. Davis has the right, if he wishes, to insist that not less than 250 shall be paid for.
Then he says :	-
As matters stood, so long as this lease was the only contract, it rested with the chief engineer to define the points along the canal at which lights were required, and from time to time to determine the number of lights. The prices and various particulars in regard, to the lights are specified by the lease.
The Order in Council of October 9, 1900, and the agreement of October 19, 1900, specify in distinct language the number of lights to be furnished. They are to be, in number, not less than 250 nor more than 270, at the discretion of the department, and the government having by this Order in Council and subsequent agreement exercised the right reserved to it under the lease of determining the number of such lights which Mr. Davis should supply, he is, X think, entitled to rely upon such Order in Council and subsequent agreement, and to say that if any lights at all are required from him on any particular night, the number of them shall be not less than 250.
I am not going to say that the Order in Council of 1900 was a proper order. I believe that possibly an arrangement could have been made at that time fixing the number of lights for the season of navigation and during the winter months. However, as we find the Order in Council fixing the minimum number of lights at 250, if Mr. Davis supplied those lights or if he was ready to supply those lights, I contend that he would be entitled to be paid for them. Under Mr. Davis's contract there was a minimum quantity of power fixed and the moment Mr. Davis was ready to deliver that power it was no fault of his if the government were not ready to receive it, and therefore I say that legally he was entitled to be paid for it and that consequently he was quite justified in filing a claim for the amount he did claim. However, as the hon. the Minister of Justice has explained the Treasury Board followed as they considered the law and they reversed the ruling of the Auditor General, but subsequently a compromise was made and under that compromise the contractor is now paid for 125 horse-power and 244 lights for the season of navigation for 100 lights during the winter months computed at 121 days. There was a good deal of criticism last session in regard to these lights during winter. I do not know whether all the members understand it, but not only are the lights necessary, but power is necessary in the winter time. It is not all necessary for the lock gates, but the weirs and sluices have to be operated during the winter months, so that some power is required in winter as well as in summer, and some lights are required



during the winter months. Now, I am glad to say that the experts who were put on this work found that it was a splendid plant. I think everybody who is familiar with the plant knows that it is a splendid plant and that the plant is in the hands of one who will certainly fill his contract with the government. Some stress has been laid on the fact that the government inserted a clause in the lease of 1896, by which they had the right to take over these works at any time. In view of that I think probably that the experts were quite right in finding that it was not unreasonable to enter into this contract for a long term of years as the government had reserved the right to determine it at any time and take over the works. I apologize for having taken up so much time, but it seemed to me that when there have been so many mis-statements in the press in regard to this matter, it was my duty to say something in regard to this work and these contracts.

I think that although it would be very unfair to ask the House to listen to me for any great length of time, I shall have the indulgence of the House in the exceptional position I occupy just now for a minute or two. I had the ambition to be an independent member on some one occasion and I always wished to vote for the government once if I possibly could. Seeing that there is no opportunity, and probably will not be an oportunity of voting with the government, entertaining the convictions I do, I am not at all sorry for standing pretty well alone to-night. I am proud of the able support of the hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who supported my arguments and I am not at all discouraged. I have the idea that it would not be a difficult matter to dispose of such arguments as have been advanced, even by gentlemen on this side of the House, if the opportunity presented itself. I hope I made it clear to the government that I only took this as a sample of many other cases. As the member for Cornwall said, there are a great number of eases which upon the face of them seem to indicate something wrong. Not only as to those I mentioned to-night, but as to others I shall court an opportunity during this session perhaps, of bringing them to the attention of the House. I expected that we would have had some argument from the governement to explain away the fact that the instrument entered into by the government in 1898 amounted to nothing more than a mere option giving Mr. Davis the right to occupy these premises at $1,000 a year, and binding the government to nothing whatever. Therefore, the government were in an easy position to get rid of that option if they thought fit, and they must not now attempt to screen themselves behind the document of 1896. I have not Mr. PRINGLE.
heard any argument to dispose of the established fact, that whereas we were committed by the government to pay upwards of $52,000, that has been reduced to $29,000 by the activity of the Auditor Generali, and the figures produced by the hon. member for Cornwall show that we are paying about full value for the service, when we pay $29,000. I do not complain of my hon. friend (Mr. Pringle) discussing this matter, although his advocacy of it was a little stronger than anything offered by the government side. Although we are apt to get a little careless about it in this House, we must remember that we are commanded to love our neighbours as ourselves, and as this work is in his own county, it follows I suppose that the hon. gentleman has a very strong affection 'for the work and for the contractor. I have no brief to defend the Auditor General. He is an appointee of the Liberal government; he has the esteem and confidence of the Liberal party in Canada. There may be reasons why the present government find him inconvenient. It is not the first time in history, that parties have promoted men to power and have afterwards been most anxious to get rid of them. It is more than whispered that the government find the guardian of the treasury inconvenient. The attempt last session to deprive the Auditor General of the undoubted powers he possesses, has not been forgotten. I shall endeavour when the opportunity occurs later on to discuss more of these Treasury Board overrulings, but in the meantime, I may say that there was absolute power on the part of the government to begin anew this contract in 1900, and by a stroke of the pen, they could have terminated the previous contract, if they wished to do so.
